1.pericope_label: But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession, and kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles’ feet

schools.summary: Gill observes that Ananias is a name common among the Jews, the same with Hananiah, and that it signifies not the humility or the affliction or the answer of the Lord, as some say, but the grace of the Lord or the Lord’s gracious one; there is, he adds, no dependence on names, for though this man’s name signified one who was in the grace and favour of God he was not so but a graceless person, as appears by what follows. It is very likely, he thinks, that he was a minister of the word, since the account of him follows upon that of Barnabas and is opposed to it, and it may be that he was one of the hundred and twenty on whom the Holy Ghost fell at Pentecost, so that though he had great gifts he had no grace; which shows that there are hypocrites among men of the greatest names and characters and in the purest churches, this first and pure church, so largely praised in the preceding chapter, not being free from them. Of the keeping back he says only that he reserved part of the price for his own use, after he had given out that he sold the possession for the service of the church. Calvin says that the things Luke has reported hitherto showed that the company gathered together under the name of Christ was rather a company of angels than of men, since it was incredible virtue that rich men should despoil themselves of their own accord, not only of their money but also of their land, that they might relieve the poor; but now he shows that Satan had invented a shift to get into that holy company, and that under colour of such excellent virtue, for he has wonderful wiles of hypocrisy to insinuate himself, and this is how he assaults the Church when he cannot prevail by open war. We must specially in this place have respect to the drift of the Holy Ghost, who meant in this history to declare first how acceptable singleness of heart is to God and what an abomination hypocrisy is in his sight, and secondly how greatly he approves the holy and pure policy and government of his Church. Luke, he says, condemns no other fault in Ananias than this, that he meant to deceive God and the Church with a feigned offering; yet there were more evils packed under this dissimulation, the contempt of God whom he feared not though he knew his own wickedness, sacrilegious defrauding because he kept back part of what he professed to be holy to God, perverse vanity and ambition because he vaunted himself before men without respect to God’s judgment, want of faith because he would never have taken this course had he not mistrusted God, the corrupting of a godly and holy order, and the hypocrisy itself, which was a great offence of itself. The act bore a goodly show, and it is no small virtue for a rich man to bestow the half of his goods upon the poor; but the sacrifices of the ungodly are an abomination to God, nor can anything please him where singleness of heart is wanting, which is why Christ made more account of the two mites offered by the widow than of the great sums of others who gave some part out of their great heaps. Calvin then draws the lesson from ambition: Ananias is ashamed not to be accounted one of the best, and therefore, though greedy of money, deprives himself of some part of his riches in order to purchase a name among men, not considering that he lies and deceives in the sight of God and that God will punish the lie; so it is that he honours the apostles’ feet more than God’s eyes, and we must take good heed that when we do well we do not seek the praise of the bystanders, Christ saying not without cause that in giving alms it is profitable for us that the left hand should not know what the right hand does.

Henry begins with the melancholy conjunction which puts a stop to the pleasant and agreeable prospect of things in the foregoing chapters, since as every man so every church in its best state has its but. The disciples were very holy and heavenly and seemed all exceedingly good, but there were hypocrites among them whose hearts were not right in the sight of God, who when they were baptized took upon them the form of godliness and denied its power; there is a mixture of bad with good in the best societies on this side heaven, and tares will grow among the wheat until the harvest. It was the praise of the disciples that they came up to the perfection Christ recommended to the rich young man, selling what they had and giving to the poor, but even that proved a cloak and cover of hypocrisy which was thought the greatest evidence of sincerity; and the signs and wonders the apostles wrought were hitherto miracles of mercy, but now comes in a miracle of judgment, an instance of severity following the instances of goodness, that God may be both loved and feared. Of the sin itself he says it is good to see husband and wife joining together in what is good, but to be confederate in evil is to be like Adam and Eve when they agreed to eat the forbidden fruit. Their fault he divides in three. They were ambitious of being thought eminent disciples and of the first rank when really they were not true disciples, wishing to pass for the most fruitful trees in Christ’s vineyard when the root of the matter was not in them, and bringing the money as Barnabas did that they might not seem behind the chief of believers but be applauded and stand fairer for preferment in a church which they perhaps thought would shortly shine in secular pomp; it is possible, he notes, for hypocrites to deny themselves in one thing in order to serve themselves in another, and it is often of fatal consequence for people to go a greater length in profession than their inward principle will admit of. They were covetous of the wealth of the world and distrustful of God and his providence, having perhaps in a pang of zeal designed to dedicate the whole and then, when the money was received, found their heart fail them, thinking it too much to part with at once and not knowing but they might want it themselves; thus they thought to serve both God and mammon, bringing part to the apostles’ feet and keeping part in their own pockets, as if there were not an all-sufficiency in God unless they retained some by way of caution-money. Their hearts were divided and so they were found faulty; they halted between two, for if they had been thorough-paced worldlings they would not have sold the possession, and if thorough-paced Christians they would not have detained part of the price. And they thought to deceive the apostles and make them believe they brought the whole, coming with as great a show of piety and devotion as any and laying the money at the apostles’ feet as if it were their all, dissembling with God and his Spirit, with Christ and his church and ministers. Henry adds that many are brought to gross lying by reigning pride and the affectation of the applause of men, particularly in works of charity to the poor, and that those who boast of good works they never did, or promise works they never do, or make the works they do more or better than they really are, come under the guilt of Ananias’s lie. Lightfoot turns to the transaction that precedes it, noting that the two apostles of the Gentiles have Gentile countries for their native soil, Paul in Cilicia and Barnabas in Cyprus, where also he sold his land; for it is a question whether he could have sold it in the land of Israel, and also whether he, being a Levite, was capable of possessing any land that had not belonged to the cities of Levi, which could not be sold in the same manner as other lands. It was not lawful, he adds, for an Israelite to part with the land of his inheritance unless constrained to it by his poverty, according as it is said that if thy brother should become poor and sell his possession; here, however, lands are sold not so much on account of their own poverty as of the poverty of others. On the keeping back he asks whether Ananias did not remember what things had been prophesied concerning the Spirit of the Messiah, that he should be made quick of scent in the fear of the Lord, with the rabbinic gloss that he smells out a man whether he be guilty or innocent, and the story of Bar-Cozbi, who reigned two years and a half and told the Rabbins he was the Messiah, and was answered that since it is written of the Messiah that he smells and judges, let them see whether he could do so also. By what apprehension of things Ananias was so deceived as to think to have deceived the Holy Ghost is not easy to conceive or guess, since he might have understood by the instance of Gehazi how quick and sagacious the spirit of a prophet is in detecting all things.

Clarke prefixes a summary of the whole chapter, from the hypocrisy of Ananias and Sapphira and their awful death, through the miracles and the increase of the Church, the imprisonment and the angel’s deliverance, the council and the apostles’ defence, Gamaliel’s advice, and the beating and the rejoicing. Of the man himself he says that we have no further account than what is recorded here, that in reference to birth and connections their names are written in the dust, and that the import of his name, the grace or mercy of the Lord, agrees very ill with his conduct. Ananias and Sapphira, he holds, were evidently persons who professed faith in Christ with the rest of the disciples: while all were making sacrifices for the present necessity they came forward among the rest, pretending to bring all the money they had got for a possession which they had sold, but keeping back a part, not being willing to trust entirely to the bounty of Providence as the others did, and thinking probably that as the whole was their own they had a right to do with it as they pleased. And so they had, he grants, for they were under no necessity to sell their possession; but the act of selling it for the ostensible purpose of bringing it into the common stock left them no further control over it nor property in it, and their pretence that the money brought was the whole produce of the sale was a direct lie in itself and an attempt to deceive the Holy Spirit, under whose influence they pretended to act, which constituted the iniquity of their sin. Wesley says it is certain that Ananias was not a believer, for all that believed were of one heart and of one soul, and that he was probably not baptized but intending now to offer himself for baptism; and of the part brought he says it was brought as if it had been the whole, perhaps with the saying that it was so.

Barnes explains that in the previous chapter the historian had given an account of the eminent liberality and sincerity of the mass of early Christians in being willing to give up their property to provide for the poor, and had mentioned the case of Barnabas as worthy of special attention, and that he now proceeds to mention a case quite as striking of insincerity and hypocrisy and of the just judgment of God upon those guilty of it. The case he calls a remarkable instance of the nature of hypocrisy, illustrating the art and cunning of the enemy of souls in attempting to corrupt the church and to pervert the religion of the gospel; hypocrisy consists in an attempt to imitate the people of God or to assume the appearance of religion in whatever form it may be manifested, and in this case religion had been manifested by great self-denial and benevolence, so that the hypocrisy of Ananias consisted in attempting to imitate that appearance and to impose in this way on the early Christians and on God. The concurrence of the wife he takes as a matter of agreement between them. The word for the possession, he notes, does not indicate whether this was land or some other property, though the next verses show it was land, and the Syriac, Arabic and Vulgate render it land; the pretence for which it was sold was doubtless to have the appearance of religion, and that it was sold could easily be known by the Christian society while it might not be so easily known for how much, whence the attempt to impose on the apostles. It is clear, he adds, that they were not under obligation to sell their property, but having sold it for the purposes of religion it became their duty, if they professed to devote the proceeds to God, to do it entirely and without any reservation. The word for keeping back he says means properly to separate or part, and then to separate surreptitiously or clandestinely for our own use a part of public property such as taxes; it is used three times in the New Testament and is rendered purloining in one of them, and here it means that they secretly kept back a part while professedly devoting all to God. The laying at the apostles’ feet was evidently an act professedly of devoting all to God, and that this was his profession or pretence is further implied in the charge that he had lied unto God. Ellicott observes that the mere act of keeping back would not in itself have been sinful, since the money was his own to give the whole or a part, but that the formal act, apparently reproducing that of Barnabas, was an acted lie, the part being offered as if it were the whole. The word for keeping back, he notes, is rendered purloining elsewhere and always carried with it the idea of stealthy and dishonest appropriation, being used in the Greek Old Testament to describe the sin of Achan. Robertson parses the verb of selling as an aorist active for a single case, and the verb of keeping back as a first aorist middle of an old verb formed from the word for afar or apart, so as to set apart or separate for oneself, occurring only here, in the following verse, and once in the Epistle to Titus. The clause about the wife he takes as a genitive absolute with the second perfect participle of the verb to know together with one, so that she knew it together with him; and the bringing of the part he parses as an aorist participle for a definite act. The praise of Joseph, he remarks, was too much for Ananias, but he was not willing to turn over all: he wanted praise for giving all and yet took care of himself by keeping some, and thus he started the Ananias Club that gave a new meaning to his lovely name.

debates: Who Ananias was: Gill thinks he may well have been a minister of the word, placed here directly after Barnabas, and perhaps even one of the hundred and twenty on whom the Spirit fell, a man with great gifts and no grace; Wesley denies he was a believer at all, since all who believed were of one heart and one soul, and supposes him not yet baptized; Clarke and Barnes treat him simply as one who professed faith along with the rest.

Where the sin lay: Ellicott and Clarke both clear the ground first, since the money was his own and keeping it back was no sin in itself, and locate the offence precisely in the acted lie by which the part was offered as the whole; Calvin agrees that Luke charges nothing else, but unpacks six further evils folded inside the dissimulation; Henry divides it into ambition, covetous distrust of providence, and the attempt to deceive the apostles.

What drove him: Henry finds both ambition and covetousness, a heart divided and halting between two; Calvin makes it ambition alone, a man ashamed not to be counted among the best and honouring the apostles’ feet more than the eyes of God; Robertson says simply that the praise of Joseph was too much for him.
outliers: Lightfoot asks whether Barnabas could lawfully have sold land inside Israel at all, and whether a Levite could hold any land outside the cities of Levi, noting that the law allowed a man to part with his inheritance only under constraint of poverty.
Lightfoot brings rabbinic material on the Messiah who smells and judges rather than judging by sight, including the challenge put to Bar-Cozbi when he claimed the title.
Robertson remarks that Ananias wanted the credit of giving all while quietly keeping some, and so founded the Ananias Club that gave a new meaning to his lovely name.
Henry observes that every man, and every church in its best state, has its but, and that tares will grow among the wheat until the harvest.
themes: kept back part of the price

3.pericope_label: But Peter said, Ananias, why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost, and to keep back part of the price of the land? Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God. And Ananias hearing these words fell down, and gave up the ghost: and great fear came on all them that heard these things. And the young men arose, wound him up, and carried him out, and buried him

schools.summary: Gill says that Peter, by divine revelation or by a spirit of discerning such as Elisha had, who knew what his servant Gehazi had done, knew what a reserve Ananias had made and called him by his name. On the following verse he insists that before it was sold the estate was his own proper property, that he had the sole right in it and could have kept it or disposed of it as he pleased, since he was not obliged to sell it; selling of possessions at this time was a voluntary thing which no man was forced to, a pure act of liberality not enjoined by the apostles, every man being left to his liberty. Of the death he says that Peter’s words detected the sin and convicted him of it, setting forth its evil nature with its aggravating circumstances, and that such power went along with them and they cut so deep that he immediately fell. Calvin asks how Peter knew the fraud and answers, undoubtedly by the revelation of the Spirit, so that Luke signifies to us that the apostles did after a sort represent God’s person and supply his room; and if the Spirit of God by the mouth of a mortal man so sorely urges a hypocrite otherwise painted with the beautiful colour of virtues, how shall the reprobate abide the voice of God himself with the sound of the trumpet when they appear before his judgment-seat. Peter points out the atrocity of the offence by his question, when he says that Satan had filled the heart of Ananias; for there is no man whose heart is not pricked with the pricks of Satan, and all men are many ways tempted, and these temptations pierce into their minds, but where Satan possesses the heart he reigns in the whole man, having as it were expelled God, and this is a sign of a reprobate, to be so addicted and given over to Satan that the Spirit of God has no place. What follows concerning lying may have a double sense, either that he falsely bore a show of the Spirit or that he lied against the Spirit; and forasmuch as the Greek word is joined with a double accusative case, and that agrees better with the context, Calvin is rather of the mind that Ananias is reprehended because he lied falsely to the Holy Ghost, which Peter confirms shortly after when he upbraids him with having lied unto God and not unto men. We must therefore take great heed, he says, that hypocrisy reign not in us, which has this wickedness proper to it, to go about to deceive God and as it were to put out the eyes of the crow, which cannot be without a disloyal and unseemly mock; and it is not without cause that Peter says the heart is possessed of Satan where this comes to pass, for who would dare, unless void of reason, so to blaspheme God. The next verse he takes to amplify the offence, because Ananias sinned being enforced by no necessity; for since it is no just excuse to have been provoked by some other means, how much worse is it to run headlong into wickedness willingly and as it were of set purpose to pull down God’s vengeance. We gather from this that no man was enforced to sell his goods or lands, since Peter says that Ananias had free liberty to keep both his land and his money, and he should nevertheless have been counted faithful though he had kept what was his own; whereby it appears that they are men destitute of their right wits who say that it is not lawful for the faithful to have anything of their own. Ananias had deceived the Church, but he ought to have considered that where two or three are gathered together in the name of Christ, he is present there as the chief governor, and he ought to have behaved himself in that assembly no otherwise than if he had seen God with his eyes; for seeing that God will reign in the Church, if we give him any reverence we must reverence religiously that rule and government which he exercises by his Word, the apostles being indeed men but not private men, because God had put them in his stead. That he who lies to the Holy Ghost is said to lie to God manifestly proves the divinity of the Holy Ghost, as Paul likewise says that we are the temples of God because his Spirit dwells in us. The death of Ananias, Calvin says, declares the force of the word, which Paul highly extols as the savour of death unto death to those who perish; he speaks indeed of the spiritual death of the soul, but there was a visible sign in the body of Ananias of that punishment which cannot be seen with the eyes of men, since he was slain neither with sword nor force nor hand but was stricken dead with the only hearing of the voice. Let the threatenings of the gospel therefore terrify us and humble us in time, lest we also feel the like effect, for what is spoken of Christ, that he shall slay the wicked with the breath of his mouth, appertains not only to the head of the wicked but to every member. If any man think it absurd that the apostle should punish Ananias bodily, Calvin answers first that this was an extraordinary thing and secondly that it was one of the gifts of the Spirit, as appears from the Epistle to the Corinthians, and as Elymas the sorcerer was afterwards stricken with blindness by Paul; Peter therefore did nothing impertinent to his function when he shot in time the dart which the Holy Ghost had given him. To those who think the punishment too cruel he answers that this comes to pass because, weighing Ananias’ sin in their own and not in God’s balance, they count that a light offence which was a most grievous crime; and to those who think it nothing so, because they see many hypocrites escape scot free daily, he answers that as God poured out visible graces upon his Church in the beginning so he declared by the visible punishment of two how horrible a judgment remains for all hypocrites who mock God and his Church, the Lord’s purpose being by punishing one to make the rest afraid, and this appertains to us also, since God meant to give all ages a lesson at that time. In the meantime, he adds, the punishment of this wicked person ought to have encouraged the godly thereafter to consecrate their goods more freely to God and the poor, since they might gather how precious alms was in God’s sight, seeing the profaning of it was so punished.

Lightfoot asks whether Peter derived the authority of sentencing this man to an immediate death from the words of our Lord about retaining sins, or whether from some immediate revelation, or both; and he observes that Peter gives here a notable instance of his own repentance and recovery after his fall, in that he who by a lie, yea even by perjury itself, had denied his Master, does such severe execution upon another for a lie of which he was guilty. On the burial he notes that the young men, having no burying cloths at hand, bind up the dead man in what fashion they can, and carrying him out of that place commit him to the earth.

Clarke observes that the verb which we translate to fill has been shown by Kypke, with many examples, to signify to instigate, excite or impel, and that it was a common belief among the heathens as well as among Jews and Christians that when a man did evil he was excited to it by the influence and malice of an evil spirit; it is strange, he remarks, that by the general consent of mankind sin against God has ever been considered so unnatural and so evil in itself that no man would commit it unless impelled by the agency of the devil. The words of Peter here prove that such an agency is not fictitious, for if there were no devil, as some wish and perhaps find it their interest to believe, or if this devil had no influence on the souls of men, Peter under the agency of the Holy Spirit would not have expressed himself in this way, since if the thing were not so it would have been the most direct means of leading the disciples into false opinions or confirming them in old prejudices. To lie to the Holy Ghost he renders as to deceive the Holy Spirit, since every lie is told with the intention to deceive and they wished to deceive the apostles and in effect that Holy Spirit under whose influence they professed to act; and since lying against the Holy Ghost is in the next verse said to be lying against God, therefore the Holy Ghost is God. The verb for keeping back he notes is used by Greek writers of purloining part of the public money, and is used here with great propriety, since the money for which the estate was sold was public property, that being the sole purpose of the sale. The falling down he renders as falling down he expired or breathed his last, and calls the received rendering a very improper translation; and he remarks two things, that the sin of this person was of no ordinary magnitude, else God would not have visited it with so signal a punishment, and that Peter must have had the power to discern the state of the heart, else he had not known the perfidy of Ananias, this power, commonly called the discernment of spirits, being one the apostles had as a particular gift, not probably always but at select times when God saw it necessary for the good of his Church. Wesley glosses the lying as to the Holy Ghost who is in us, and notes that here was the first instance of keeping back and the first attempt to bring propriety of goods into the Christian Church. On the following verse he grants that whosoever among the Christians had houses or lands sold them and laid the price at the apostles’ feet, but adds that it was in Ananias’ own choice to be a Christian or not, and consequently either to sell his land or to keep it, and that it does not appear he professed himself a Christian when he sold it; the closing charge he paraphrases as asking why he should so profanely dissemble on so solemn an occasion, and observes that hence the Godhead of the Holy Ghost evidently appears, since lying to him is lying to God. Of the death he says the severity was not only just, considering the complication of vain glory, covetousness, fraud and impiety which the action contained, but was also wise and gracious, since it would effectually deter others from following the example; it was likewise a convincing proof of the upright conduct of the apostles in managing the sums with which they were entrusted, and in general of their divine mission, for none can imagine that Peter would have had the assurance to pronounce, much less the power to execute, such a sentence, if he had been guilty himself of a fraud of the same kind.

Barnes says Peter could have known this only by revelation, since it was the manifest design of Ananias to deceive and there was no other way of detecting him; as it was an instance of enormous wickedness and very important to detect and punish, it was made known to Peter directly by God. Great deeds of wickedness are in the Scripture traced to the influence and temptation of Satan, and especially is Satan called the father of lies, so that an act of falsehood is with great propriety traced to him; but the sin of Ananias consisted in his yielding to the temptation, and nowhere in the Bible are men supposed to be free from guilt because they have been tempted, God requiring them to resist. A man’s heart is full of a thing when he is intent on it or strongly impelled to it, and the expression here means that he was strongly impelled to this crime. On the name of the Holy Ghost he argues at length that a distinction between the Father and the Spirit is here recognised: if no such distinction were intended it is remarkable that Peter did not use the customary name of God, and that he guarded it so carefully as to denote that the offence was against the Holy Ghost and the Spirit of the Lord; the name used is the one employed throughout Scripture for the Third Person as distinct from the Father; Peter meant to designate an offence against the Person by whom he and the other apostles were inspired, who was sent by the Father and appointed to a particular work; and the sin here committed was of that peculiar magnitude which the sin against the Holy Ghost is uniformly represented to have. From this he draws two conclusions: that the Holy Ghost is a distinct Person, since sin cannot be committed against an attribute of God or an influence from God, for we cannot lie to wisdom or power or goodness, and sin is committed against a being; and that the Holy Ghost is divine, since he is here represented as able to search the heart and detect hypocrisy, and is expressly called God in the next verse. On that verse he explains that as long as the property remained unsold there was no obligation to sell it, those who did so doing it voluntarily, and that even after the sale there was no obligation to devote the money in this way, which shows that the offence was peculiarly aggravated, since Ananias was not compelled to sell and could not even plead that he was obliged to dispose of it and tempted to withhold. The charge that he had not lied unto men he takes to mean not unto men only, since the principal magnitude of the offence was that he had attempted to deceive God, as David saw his sin as committed against God to be so enormous that he lost sight of it as an offence to man. Of the death he says it is evidently to be regarded as a judgment of God for the sin and not the act of Peter, clearly designed to show God’s abhorrence of it; yet though it was the act of God it does not follow that it was not in connection with the usual laws by which he governs men, since the sin was one of great aggravation, suddenly and unexpectedly detected, and the shock of the charge would strike the conscience with horror, and instances have occurred where such a shock destroyed the vital powers at once. He renders the phrase for expiring as simply he died, calling the received rendering unhappy. Ellicott says the narrative is obviously intended to leave the impression that Peter’s knowledge of the fact came from a supernatural insight, he having that prophetic gift which gave him insight into the hearts of men, so that through this outward show of generous devotion he read the baseness and the lie, and traced that evil to its fountain-head; like the sin of Judas, it had in it a malignant subtlety of evil which implied the perversion of conscience and will just at the moment when they seemed to be, and may actually have been, on the point of attaining a higher perfection than before, and the question why implies that resistance to the temptation had been possible, since had he resisted the Tempter he would have fled from him. The words about lying he says admit of two tenable interpretations, either as lying against him who dwelt in the Apostles whom Ananias was seeking to deceive, or as against him who was the Searcher of the secrets of all hearts, his own included, and who was grieved by this resistance in one called to a higher life; the apparent parallelism of the clause in the following verse favours the first, but there is in the Greek a distinction obviously made deliberately between the structure of the verb in the two sentences, since here it is used with the accusative of the direct object, so that the meaning is to cheat or deceive the Holy Spirit, and there with the dative, to speak a lie not to men but to God, which gives a sense compatible with the second. The special intensity of the sin, he adds, consisted in its being against the light and knowledge with which the human spirit had been illumined by the divine, the attempt to deceive those in whom that Spirit dwelt coming in afterwards as a secondary aggravation. On the next verse he says fresh circumstances are pressed home as depriving the act of every possible excuse: Ananias had not been bound by any rule of the Church to such a gift, at every stage he was free to act as he thought best, and had he brought part as part, or even brought nothing, he would have been free from any special blame; as it was, the attempt to obtain the reputation of saintliness without the reality of sacrifice involved him in the guilt at once of sacrilege, though there had been no formal consecration, and of perjury, though there had been no formulated oath. The parallelism between the two verses he says has often been used, and perfectly legitimately, as a proof that while the Apostles thought of the Spirit as sent by the Father and therefore distinct in his personality, they yet did not shrink from speaking of him as God. Of the death he notes that Peter’s words, while they press home the intensity of the guilt, do not contain any formal sentence, and that in such a case we may rightly trace that union of natural causation and divine purpose which we express in the familiar phrase about the visitation of God, since the shame and agony of detection and the horror of a conscience not yet dead were enough to paralyse the powers of life; retribution is not less a divine act because it comes, through the working of divine laws, as the natural consequence of the sin which draws it down. It was necessary, he says reverently, that this worst corruption of the best should be manifestly condemned on its first appearance by a divine judgment; and we must remember that there is a silence we may not dare to break as to all but the visible judgment, the dominant apostolic idea of such punishments being that men were delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. Robertson notes that the verb for filling is the very one used of the filling by the Holy Spirit, that Satan the adversary is the father of lies, that he had entered into Judas and now has filled the heart of Ananias with a lie; he parses the infinitive of lying as an aorist middle of purpose with the accusative of the person as often in Greek writers though only here in the New Testament with this verb, the usual dative of the person appearing in the next verse. Of that verse he adds that the devil filled his heart, but all the same Ananias did it too and is wholly responsible. The falling down he parses as an aorist participle, fallen all of a sudden while listening, and the expiring as a late verb meaning to breathe out, found in the New Testament only here and twice more; it is needless, he says, to blame Peter for the death of Ananias, who had brought the end upon himself, since it was the judgment of God, and physically the nervous shock could have caused the collapse.

Cyril turns the episode into an argument for the Spirit’s presence and knowledge: Peter was not with Ananias and Sapphira when they sold their possessions, but he was present by the Spirit, and when he asks why Satan has filled his heart to lie to the Holy Ghost there was no accuser and no witness — whence then knew he what had happened? Whiles it remained, was it not thine own, and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power, why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? The unlettered Peter, he says, through the grace of the Spirit learnt what not even the wise men of the Greeks had known. He finds the like in the case of Elisha, who having freely healed the leprosy of Naaman saw Gehazi receive the reward of another’s achievement and bestow the money in a dark place; but the darkness is not hidden from the Saints, and when he came Elisha questioned him as Peter questioned here.

debates: What the lying governs: Ellicott sets out both readings, an offence against the Spirit dwelling in the Apostles or against the Spirit as searcher of the man’s own heart, and lets the deliberate change of case — accusative here, dative in the next verse — tip him toward the second; Calvin weighs the same two alternatives and comes down the other way on the same kind of evidence, since the Greek verb takes a double accusative; Robertson notes the difference of case without pressing it either way.

Whose act the death was: Barnes insists it was God’s judgment and not Peter’s act, while allowing that natural means may have served; Robertson says it is needless to blame Peter, the nervous shock being enough; Ellicott observes that Peter pronounced no formal sentence at all; Calvin defends the apostle positively, that he shot in time the dart the Holy Ghost had given him, as Paul afterwards struck Elymas blind.

Whether the punishment was too severe: Calvin answers two objections at once, that those who call it cruel weigh the sin in their own balance and not God’s, and that those who think it slight because hypocrites escape daily miss that God showed in two what awaits all; Wesley calls the severity just and also wise and gracious, deterring imitators and proving the apostles’ integrity with the money entrusted to them.
outliers: Lightfoot observes that the man who had denied his Master with a lie, and with perjury, is the one who here executes another for lying — a notable instance of his own repentance and recovery.
Clarke argues from Peter’s wording that the devil’s agency is not fictitious, since the Spirit would not have led the disciples into a false opinion by speaking so if no such agency existed.
Cyril remarks that the unlettered Peter, through the grace of the Spirit, learnt what not even the wise men of the Greeks had known.

Ellicott refuses to speculate beyond the visible judgment, recalling that the apostolic idea of such punishments was that men were delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit might be saved.

7.pericope_label: And it was about the space of three hours after, when his wife, not knowing what was done, came in. And Peter answered unto her, Tell me whether ye sold the land for so much? And she said, Yea, for so much. Then Peter said unto her, How is it that ye have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? behold, the feet of them which have buried thy husband are at the door, and shall carry thee out. Then fell she down straightway at his feet, and yielded up the ghost: and the young men came in, and found her dead, and, carrying her forth, buried her by her husband. And great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things

schools.summary: Gill accounts for the three hours by the burial, since the burying places of the Jews were without the city and, if they were as distant from other cities as they were from the cities of the Levites, they were above a mile and a half off. Of Peter answering he notes that she might have been inquiring for her husband, though such a way of speaking was common with the Jews when nothing goes before to which the answer is made. That husband and wife should agree together in things civil, honest and lawful and in religious matters is very commendable, he says, but to agree in a fraud and in a lie is very dreadful; and of the death he says only that she fell in like manner and by the same hand of God as her husband before, the fear of the church being still more increased by it. Calvin says the punishment of Sapphira contains no new thing save that the example was the more confirmed by it, and that it came to pass by the certain providence of God that the Church should see apart the obstinate wickedness and treacherous mind of them both; since their faults were alike they might have been known together, but this was more fit and profitable for the Church, that they might severally betray their own wickedness. Nor was Sapphira provoked by the sight of her husband to dissemble, as it often falls out, so that the fault could be ascribed to shamefacedness, but of her own accord and pricked forward by no other means she shows herself no better than he. We see, he adds, that God does not punish her by sudden impulse but first tries the matter thoroughly, lest he should send vengeance upon any save the obstinate and those who cut themselves off from pardon; for although Sapphira knew the matter was hidden, she ought to have been stricken by this question of Peter no otherwise than if she had been cited before the judgment-seat of God. She has a time granted her to repent, and this is as it were a calm inviting unto repentance; but by proceeding so securely she declares that she was incurable, because she is touched with no fear of God. Hereby we are taught to labour diligently to bring sinners into the way, for the Spirit of God keeps this moderation; but when stubbornness and the stubborn contempt of God is added to the offence, it is high time to punish, and those men are too arrogant who are displeased with the rigour of God. So many circumstances, he says, prove that the two were not worthy of one death only: hypocrisy is of itself abominable to God; their determination to lie unto God arose from great contempt, in that they did not fear Christ, the chief Governor of those among whom they were; it was ungodliness joined with impudency, since so they could escape shame among men they cared not to deny their manifest wickedness to God; and their stubborn denial made up the heap and measure. That innumerable hypocrites daily mock God and the Church without being punished with death he has already answered: since God is the only Judge of the world it belongs to him to punish every man at his pleasure, and we must not prescribe to him a certain manner of punishment, while the greatness of the spiritual judgment which is as yet hid has been set before us in the bodily punishment of two, as in a mirror; for if we consider what it is to be cast into eternal fire, we shall not judge that to fall down dead before men is the greatest evil of all. Of the tempting he says that Peter utters in other words what he had said before, that they mocked God irreverently, but says they tempted the Spirit because they had cunningly packed their fraud as if the Spirit of God were not the knower of hearts; for it was a point of too great carelessness, seeing the one made the other privy to their wickedness, to make their match between themselves having as it were excluded God, since the Scripture says that God is tempted either when his power is taken from him or the knowledge of all things is denied him. By the Spirit, he adds, is meant that Spirit which governed the Church by the apostles, since when Christ says that the Spirit when he comes shall judge the world he notes no other kind of authority than that which he exercises by the ministry of the Church. Of the fear he says the punishment of one was a lesson to all, and plainly distinguishes a double fear: the Church feared, because the faithful never so perfectly fear God but that they profit yet more when admonished by his judgments, so that by all the punishments we read of and daily see God calls us back from the enticements and liberty of sinning, our flesh needing to be bridled every now and then because one bridle will scarce serve the turn; and there was another manner of fear in the strangers, yet no such fear as brought them to the sincere worship of God, though it was such as caused them to give the glory to God.

Clarke insists that it was not by Peter’s words, nor through Peter’s prayers, nor through shame, nor through remorse that this guilty pair died, but by an immediate judgment of God. The question of the salvation of Ananias and Sapphira, he says, has been not a little agitated, and most seem inclined to hope that though their sin was punished by this awful display of the divine judgment, mercy was extended to their souls; for his own part he thinks their sin was what is elsewhere called a sin unto death, a sin which must be punished with temporal death or the death of the body, while mercy was extended to the soul. It was right in this infant state of the Church, he argues, to show God’s displeasure against deceit, fraud and hypocrisy, for had this guilty pair been permitted to live after they had done this evil, the long-suffering would infallibly have been abused by others, and instead of leading them who had sinned to repentance might have led them to hardness of heart by causing them to presume on the mercy of God; that hypocrisy may be afraid to show her face, God makes these two an example of his justice, but because they had not the ordinary respite we may presume that God extended mercy to them, though cut off almost in the act of sin. Their case, however, cannot become a precedent, allowing them to have received mercy, because those who have seen in this case the severity of God must expect much sorer punishment if, with such an example before their eyes, they should presume on the mercy of their Maker, since this would be doing evil that good might come, and the perdition of such would be just. Of the fear he says this judgment answered the end for which it was inflicted, a deeply religious fear occupying every mind, so that hypocrisy and deception were banished from this holy assembly; and he sets out, following Doddridge, a native specimen of a New Testament Church, called by the Gospel, grafted into Christ by baptism, animated by love, united by all kinds of fellowship, and disciplined by the exemplary punishment of hypocrites. Wesley exclaims over the interval, how precious a space, since the woman had a longer time for repentance; and of the last verse he says this is the first time the Church is mentioned, and here is a native specimen of a New Testament Church, which is a company of men called by the Gospel, grafted into Christ by baptism, animated by love, united by all kind of fellowship, and disciplined by the death of Ananias and Sapphira.

Barnes observes that as Sapphira had been no less guilty than her husband, so it was ordered in the providence of God that the same judgment should come upon both. Of her answer he says that the sum named was true, in that this amount had been received for the land, but that it was also true that a larger sum had been received, and that it is as really a falsehood to deceive in this manner as it would have been to affirm that they received much more than they actually did; falsehood consists in making an erroneous representation of a thing in any way for the purpose of deceiving, and this species is much more common than an open and bold lie declaring what is in no sense true. To tempt he glosses as to try, to endeavour to impose on or to deceive, that is to act as if the Spirit of the Lord could not detect the crime; and the feet at the door he explains as near at hand, the dead being buried without the walls of cities, so that the space of three hours had elapsed before the young men returned. The announcement that they should carry her out shows, he says, that it was by divine interposition that their lives were taken, the judgment being in immediate connection with the crime and designed as an expression of the divine displeasure. Why they were punished in this severe and awful manner he answers in five considerations: that the crime was atrocious, committed knowingly and without excuse, and that it was important that sudden and exemplary punishment should follow it, since the society of Christians was just then organised and was designed to be a pure society; that God has often in a solemn manner shown his abhorrence of hypocrisy and insincerity, no small part of the Saviour’s preaching being employed in detecting the hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees, so that at the beginning of the Christian church it was important by a decided act to impress upon the church and the world the danger and guilt of hypocrisy, laying the bodies of Ananias and Sapphira in the path of every hypocrite who would enter; that the apostles were just then establishing their authority and claimed to be under the influence of inspiration, so that if they could be easily imposed on it would destroy their claim, while detecting hypocrifty where it was most artfully concealed established the divine authority of their message; that the case does not stand alone in the New Testament, as the case of Elymas shows; and that neither does it stand alone in the history of the world, since acts of judgment as sudden and decided sometimes occur in providence, so that the narrative cannot be objected to as improbable until all such cases are disposed of. From the whole he draws a series of reflections, that God searches the heart and judges the motives of men rather than the external act; that fraud and hypocrisy will be detected, if not in this life then in the day when the secrets of all hearts are revealed; that the case illustrates the power of conscience; and above all that there is guilt in attempting to impose upon God in regard to property, since there is no subject in which men are more liable to hypocrisy or more apt to keep back a part. Christians profess to devote all that they have to God, and yet, he asks, has the sin of Ananias ceased in the church, when so many professing Christians give nothing really to God, contribute nothing for the poor and needy, and would devote millions to their own gratification and their families but not a penny for tribute to God; on no point, he concludes, should Christians more faithfully examine themselves than in regard to the professed devotion of their property to God. Ellicott renders the opening literally as an interval of about three hours, and says the word for Peter answering does not necessarily imply a previous questioning, though it is probable enough that she came to inquire why her husband had not returned home, perhaps expecting to find him high in honour. The question asked by Peter, he says, gave her an opening for repentance: it had been in her power to save her husband by a word of warning protest, and it was now in her power to clear her own conscience by confession, but she misses the one opportunity as she had misused the other, the lie which they had agreed upon coming glibly from her lips so that the irrevocable word is spoken. To tempt the Spirit of the Lord he explains as to try or test whether the Spirit that dwelt in the Apostles was really a discerner of the secrets of men’s hearts, and notes that the phrase for the Spirit of the Lord is probably used in its Old Testament sense, the combination being rare in the New Testament and common in the Old. In the announcement of the coming judgment he observes that the foretelling tended to work out its own completion, and that to all the shame and agony which had fallen on Ananias there was now added for her the bitter thought of her husband’s death as in some sense caused by her, inasmuch as she might have prevented the crime that led to it, the prophetic insight given to Peter having taught him that the messengers whose footsteps he already heard had another task of a like nature before them. Of the last verse he notes that, with one doubtful exception, this is the first occurrence of the word for church since the two instances in which our Lord had used it by anticipation; its frequent use in the Greek version for the assembly or congregation of Israel, and its associations with the political life of Greece as applied to assemblies every member of which was a full citizen, made it a natural and fitting word for the new society, and the use by our Lord of the actual Greek word or of the corresponding Aramaic term stamped it with his sanction. Its occurrence here, he suggests, is perhaps an indication of the increase of the Hellenistic element among the disciples; and the sudden startling death of the pair naturally tended to give a new prominence to the society, the rulers of which were seen to be clothed with supernatural powers, so that the fear which fell upon all who heard led them in part to draw near with reverence and in part to shrink back in awe. Robertson renders the opening as, now there came an interval of about three hours, and notes that the following construction is characteristic of Luke’s style in his Gospel; the participle for not knowing he parses as a feminine perfect active. The sum he takes as a genitive of price, and suggests that Peter perhaps pointed to the pile of money at the apostles’ feet. The verb of agreeing he parses as a first aorist passive used impersonally with the dative, so that it was agreed together by you, quoting the rendering that their souls were allured together respecting this deceit; and the tempting of the Spirit of the Lord he says was close to the unpardonable sin, which was attributing the manifest work of the Holy Spirit to Beelzebub. The feet he calls a graphic picture, drawn by Peter as he heard the steps of the young men at the door. Her falling immediately he takes as marking the death as supernatural like her husband’s, and the phrase about her husband as meaning face to face with him. Of the church he notes that here the word appears for the first time in Acts of the believers in Jerusalem, having twice appeared in the Gospels, once of the whole body of believers and once of a local body, while later it is used of the congregation of Israel and even of a public assembly at Ephesus; already, however, it is applied to the church which Saul was persecuting in their homes when not assembled, so that the etymological meaning of assembly disappears, the church being now the scattered saints hiding in their separate homes. The whole body of believers in Jerusalem and all who heard of the fate of the pair were in awe and dread, and it was already a dangerous thing to be a follower of Christ unless one was willing to walk straight.

Cyril sets Peter’s question beside Elisha’s to Gehazi, whom he asks whence he comes, not in ignorance but in sorrow: from darkness art thou come, and to darkness shalt thou go, for thou hast sold the cure of the leper and the leprosy is thy heritage. I, he makes the prophet say, have fulfilled the bidding of him who said, freely ye have received, freely give; but thou hast sold this grace, receive now the condition of the sale. And what says Elisha to him but, went not mine heart with thee? I was here shut in by the body, but the spirit which has been given me of God saw even the things afar off and showed me plainly what was doing elsewhere. Seest thou, Cyril asks, how the Holy Ghost not only rids of ignorance but invests with knowledge, and how he enlightens men’s souls?

debates: What became of Ananias and Sapphira: Clarke raises the question nobody else raises, reports that most incline to hope mercy was extended to their souls, and argues that theirs was a sin unto death in the strict sense, the body punished while the soul was spared — while warning that the case cannot serve as a precedent for anyone presuming on mercy after seeing such severity.

What the word for church signals here: Ellicott takes its appearance as significant, traces it through the Greek Old Testament and the civic assemblies of Greece, and suspects it marks the growth of the Hellenistic element among the disciples; Robertson observes that the etymological sense of a gathering is already fading, since the same word is soon used of saints hiding in their separate homes.

What the fear amounted to: Calvin separates two, the fear of the faithful, who never fear God so perfectly but that his judgments teach them more, and the fear of strangers, which fell short of sincere worship though it made them give God the glory; Ellicott divides it between those who drew near with reverence and those who shrank back in awe; Clarke says simply that hypocrisy and deception were banished from the assembly.
outliers: Wesley calls the three hours a precious space, since the woman had the longer time for repentance.
Calvin notes that Sapphira was not shamed into the lie by seeing her husband tell it, as often happens, so that not even bashfulness can be pleaded in her defence.
Robertson judges the act close to the unpardonable sin of ascribing the manifest work of the Holy Spirit to Beelzebub, and pictures Peter hearing the footsteps at the door as he spoke.
Barnes turns the case on his own readers, asking whether the sin of Ananias has ceased in a church where men will devote millions to their own gratification and not a penny for tribute to God.
themes: tempting the Spirit of the Lord
great fear upon all the church

12.pericope_label: And by the hands of the apostles were many signs and wonders wrought among the people; (and they were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch. And of the rest durst no man join himself to them: but the people magnified them. And believers were the more added to the Lord, multitudes both of men and women.) Insomuch that they brought forth the sick into the streets, and laid them on beds and couches, that at the least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them. There came also a multitude out of the cities round about unto Jerusalem, bringing sick folks, and them which were vexed with unclean spirits: and they were healed every one

schools.summary: Gill takes the signs and wonders to have been wrought by the apostles as instruments, or through the imposition of their hands, many miraculous cures and other extraordinary actions being performed. Of the rest who durst not join he canvasses several senses: they may be those without the church, either the profane and persecuting sort who durst not come nigh the apostles for fear of being struck dead, as the Ethiopic version suggests by reading that no man any more durst restrain them from preaching, or the better sort who attended the word and, whether real believers or hypocrites, durst not join themselves because of what had happened; but this last sense, he says, seems contradicted by the following verse. Rather he takes them to be those within the church, not only its private members but the ministers of the word, of which number Ananias might have been. The increase he reads as a great addition of such as were true believers, so far was the case of Ananias and Sapphira from hindering it; and he notes that the Ethiopic, Arabic, Syriac and Vulgate versions all construe the words unto the Lord with believers rather than with the adding. The sick, he says, were brought out by those who had them in their houses, either into the streets, as our version and the Alexandrian copy read, or in every street in Jerusalem, waiting for the apostles as they came, to receive a cure from them. Calvin says the apostle returns to miracles of another sort, more proper to the gospel, whereby Christ declares not only his power but also his goodness, that he may allure men to himself with the sweetness of his grace, since he came to save the world and not to condemn it; so that in healing the sick and delivering others from devils these benefits done to the body represent the spiritual grace of Christ and agree with his genuine office, whereas the fearful sign shown in Ananias and Sapphira came to pass extraordinarily and was as it were accidental. Luke says the Church was increased by miracles because they are subservient to faith, to prepare some and confirm others, whereby it is proved again that miracles must never be separated from the word. The multitude of the miracles is shown by the sick being brought forth everywhere to be healed, for God meant thus to set forth the gospel of his Son, especially at the beginning, that he might testify to the Jews that the restoring of all things so often promised was present. The couches he explains as certain little beds in which the men of old were wont to rest at noon, the sick being laid in them because they might the more easily be carried out. He gathers that the believers were wont to meet together at certain hours, not only for doctrine and prayers’ sake but that they might win others to the Lord as occasion was given, since every man lived at home in his own house but they had their meetings there; and no body of the Church, he says, can otherwise continue, for if every man will be his own teacher and pray apart by himself, and if there be no meetings and assemblies, however excellently the Church be ordered and appointed it must needs decay and come to nought. That they were all of one mind he takes as showing that they all kept that order willingly, no man being so disordered as to keep himself within private walls neglecting the public assembly, wherein they showed a token not only of modesty but also of constancy, since they could not do this without danger, the place being so famous, so that their agreement to put themselves in hazard was the more worthy of commendation. Of the fear that kept others back he says this was the second fruit of the miracles, in that those who believed not, being convicted by the excellent power of God, dare not despise the apostles but are rather enforced to reverence the Church. That men terrified by miracles should flee from God and his people might seem absurd, but he answers that they were hindered through their own fault, since God calls us to himself by miracles, and whosoever go not so far as willingly to embrace the grace of God which shines in them are hindered by their own perverse and evil conscience; yet this is some fruit, that God wrings some fear out of them. Luke ascribes this not only to the miracle but comprehends all together which might increase the dignity of the Church, since all things were so ordered that a certain divine majesty shone there and they differed from others no less than angels from men; for there is a secret majesty in holy discipline and in sincere godliness which binds even the wicked whether they will or no. But we know not at this day of what sort the same is, he laments; rather we cause ourselves to be despised together with the gospel through our profane liberty of evil living. He notes further that Luke here speaks of men who were indifferent and not of the worst sort, since there were many at Jerusalem whom neither the reverence of signs nor the angelic holiness of the godly could move; he means moderate men in whom there is some seed of the fear of God, like certain in our own day whom the vanity of the world keeps back from submitting their necks to the yoke of Christ, yet who, because they smell something divine in our doctrine, dare not despise it; and we may see in what deadly snares Satan entangles all who have not the Spirit of Christ, that they not only fear to provide for themselves but purposely avoid the remedies offered them, seeing and approving what is holy and profitable and yet being carried headlong to what is worse or waxing drowsy in their filthiness.

Henry gives a general account of the miracles, many miracles of mercy for one of judgment, the gospel power now returning to its proper channel of mercy and grace, God having come out of his place to punish and now returning to his mercy-seat again; the miracles proved their divine mission, being not a few but many, of divers kinds and often repeated, signs and wonders confessedly signs of a divine presence and power, and done not in a corner but among the people, who were at liberty to enquire into them and would have discovered any fraud or collusion. The first effect he finds in the church being kept together and confirmed: they met in the temple, in the open place called Solomon’s porch, and it was strange that the rulers of the temple suffered them to keep their meeting there, but God inclined their hearts to tolerate them a while for the more convenient spreading of the gospel, and those who permitted buyers and sellers could not for shame prohibit such preachers and healers. They met in public worship, so early was the institution of religious assemblies observed; and they were there with one accord, unanimous in doctrine, worship and discipline, with no discontent or murmuring about the death of Ananias and Sapphira, as there was against Moses and Aaron about the death of Korah and his company; the separation of hypocrites by distinguishing judgments, he observes, should make the sincere cleave so much the closer to each other and to the gospel ministry. The second effect was the respect gained by the apostles, the other ministers keeping their distance and acknowledging their superiority, since though others were endued with the Holy Ghost and spoke with tongues none of them at that time did such signs and wonders; and all the people magnified them and had them in great veneration, though the chief priests vilified them and did all they could to make them contemptible. The apostles, he notes, were far from magnifying themselves, transmitting the glory of all they did faithfully to Christ, and yet the people magnified them, for those that humble themselves shall be exalted. The third effect was the increase of the church: believers were added to the Lord Jesus, joined to him and so to his mystical body, from which nothing can separate us but that which cuts us off from Christ, and additions will still be made till the number of the elect is accomplished; and notice is taken of the conversion of women as well as men, more notice than generally was in the Jewish church, in which they neither received the sign of circumcision nor were obliged to attend the solemn feasts, the court of the women being one of the outer courts of the temple. The fourth was the multitude of patients: in the city they brought forth their sick into the streets, since the priests would probably not suffer them to be brought into Solomon’s porch and the apostles had not leisure to go to all their houses, and laid them on beds and couches because they were too weak to go or stand, that at least Peter’s shadow might overshadow some of them; and it should seem it had the desired effect, as the woman’s touch of the hem of Christ’s garment had, and in this the word of Christ was fulfilled that greater works than these should they do. Peter comes between them and the sun and so heals them, cutting them off from a dependence upon creature sufficiency as insufficient, that they may expect help only from that Spirit of grace with whom he was filled. If such miracles were wrought by Peter’s shadow, Henry adds, we have reason to think they were so by the other apostles, as by the handkerchiefs from Paul’s body, both no doubt with an actual intention in the minds of the apostles thus to heal; so that it is absurd to infer hence a healing virtue in the relics of saints that are dead and gone, since we read not of any cured by the relics of Christ himself after he was gone, as certainly we should if there had been any such thing. In the country towns multitudes came to Jerusalem bringing sick folks afflicted in body and those vexed with unclean spirits, troubled in mind, and they were healed every one, distempered bodies and distempered minds being set to rights; thus opportunity was given to the apostles both to convince people’s judgment of the heavenly origin of their doctrine and to engage their affections by a specimen of its beneficial tendency to the welfare of this lower world. Lightfoot asks who these should be of whom none durst join himself to the apostles, and answers that they were certainly those of the number of the hundred and twenty, excepting the twelve apostles; of this number he presumes Ananias might be one, and the rest, being terrified by the fate of one of their own order, conceived so great a dread and reverence for the apostles that they durst not join with them as their equals. He asks further why the shadow of Peter more than the rest of the apostles, who shared an equal authority and power of miracles with him, and answers first that it must be supposed the sick were not brought out in their beds into the streets unless they had first seen Peter or were assured that he must pass by, and secondly that it is a question whether they who brought out their sick knew any other of the apostles besides Peter, having heard him speaking and seen him doing.

Clarke notes that the verse about the signs and wonders should be read with the one about the sick in the streets, to which it properly belongs. On those who durst not join he reports Dr Lightfoot’s view that the hundred and twenty are intended, of whom he supposes Ananias to have been one, and who, seeing such wonders wrought by the apostles, were afraid to associate themselves with them in any way of equality, since they saw that God put peculiar honour upon them; but he prefers Calmet’s more rational observation that the Jewish nation was then divided into many different sects which entertained widely different opinions on various articles, and that since the apostles adopted none of these jarring sentiments none of the different sects dared to join themselves to them, neither Pharisees, Sadducees, nor Herodians as such being found in this simple, holy Church. The people, he adds, felt the force and power of the apostles’ doctrine and magnified them, no more attending to the teaching of the others, since the apostles taught them as men having authority and not as the scribes and Pharisees, and this irritated the high priest and his Sadducean council and led to the measures that follow. Of the believers he sets out nine articles which they credited: the divine mission of Christ, that he was the Messiah, that he died for their sins, that he rose again, that he ascended into heaven, that he sent down the gift of the Holy Spirit, that he ever appears in the presence of God for them, that it is he who gives repentance and remission of sins, and that it is he by whom the world is to be judged; these were simple articles, of the truth of which they had the fullest evidence. Wesley glosses the all as all the believers, says that none of the rest, no formalists or hypocrites, durst join themselves in an outward show only like Ananias and Sapphira, and adds that so much the more were true believers added, because unbelievers kept at a distance.

Barnes says the verse about the signs should be read in connection with the one about the sick, and that those in Solomon’s porch were doubtless there for the purpose of worship, not constantly but at the regular periods, with two designs, to join in the public worship of God in the usual manner with the people, since they did not design to leave the temple service, and to have opportunity to preach to the people assembled there, so that in the presence of the great multitudes who came up to worship they could make known the doctrines of Jesus and confirm them by miracles. Of the rest he reports and weighs the interpretations: Lightfoot supposes the remainder of the hundred and twenty, of whom Ananias had been one, and that they feared to put themselves on an equality with the apostles, which Barnes calls far-fetched; Kuinöel supposes those who had not already joined the apostles, whether Christians or Jews, deterred by the fate of Ananias; while others suppose the rich men, or the men of authority and influence among the Jews, of whom Ananias was one, and that they were deterred by that fate. This last he calls by far the most probable, for four reasons: because there is an evident contrast between them and the common people, who magnified the apostles; because the fate of Ananias was fitted to have this effect on the rich and great; because similar instances had occurred before, in which the great, though they believed on Jesus, were afraid to come forth publicly and profess him before men; and because the phrase the rest sometimes denotes that which is more excellent or more important. The rich and the great then, as now, stood aloof and were deterred by fear or shame from professing attachment to the Lord Jesus, while the mass of the nation honoured the apostles and regarded them with reverence. Believers he calls the name by which Christians were designated, because one of the main things distinguishing them was the belief that Jesus was the Christ, and takes it as incidental proof that none should join themselves to the church who are not believers in heart and life. The effect of all things, he says, was to increase the number of converts, their persecutions, their preaching and the judgment of God all tending to impress the people; and though the judgment had the effect of deterring hypocrites and producing awe and caution, the number of true converts was increased, for an effort to keep the church pure by wholesome discipline, by cutting off unworthy members however rich or honoured, so far from weakening its true strength has a tendency greatly to increase its numbers as well as its purity, since men will not seek to enter a corrupt church or regard it as worth any thought to be connected with a society that does not endeavour to be pure. The two words for what the sick were laid on he distinguishes as the soft and valuable beds on which the rich commonly lay and the coarse hard couches on which the poor used to lie, so that the rich as well as the poor were laid in the path of the apostles. Of the shadow he says they were laid in the path so that it might pass over them as Peter walked, and that perhaps the sun was near setting and his lengthened shadow might be thrown afar across the way; they were not able to approach him because of the crowd, and imagined that if they could anyhow come under his influence they might be healed. The sacred writer, he is careful to add, does not say that any were healed in this way, nor that they were commanded to do it, but simply states the impression on the minds of the people that it might be, and whether they were healed by this is left for us merely to conjecture; a somewhat similar instance is recorded later where it is expressly said that the sick were healed by contact with handkerchiefs and aprons brought from the body of Paul. Though there is no evidence that any were healed in this way, he concludes, it shows the full belief of the people that Peter had the power of working miracles, he being supposed eminently endowed with it because the lame man in the temple had been healed by him and because he had been most prominent in addressing the people. Ellicott notes that the portico was at all times a favourite place of resort for teachers, and that though the chronology of this period is still left somewhat indefinite, assuming some months to have passed since the Day of Pentecost, what is now related would be in the winter, when that portico, as facing the east and catching the morning sunlight, was more than usually frequented. Of the rest he says we are left to conjecture who these were, contrasted as they are with the Apostles on one side and with the people on the other: does it mean that the Apostles stood aloof in an isolated majesty so that none of the other disciples dared associate himself with them, or is this Luke’s way of speaking of the Pharisees and other teachers, who also resorted to the portico but, as in the days of our Lord’s ministry, had not the courage to attach themselves to those with whom they really sympathised? The latter view, he says, seems every way the more probable, and so the passage stands parallel with those which tell how the people heard our Lord gladly and came early to hear him. Added to the Lord he takes in its definite New Testament sense for the Lord Jesus; and the mention of women he says forms an introduction to the dissensions connected with the widows in the following chapter, and is itself characteristic of Luke as a writer who had seen and known the effect of the new Religion in raising women to a higher life, and whose knowledge of its history was in great measure derived from them, as later women are named among the sufferers in the first general persecution. Robertson parses the verb of the signs as an imperfect middle, wrought from time to time, and notes the adverb for with one accord as an old word occurring in the New Testament only in Acts, with all added here. Durst he parses as an imperfect of a verb meaning not to shun through fear but boldly to take a stand, and observes that the fate of Ananias and Sapphira continued to hold many in check, so that the outsiders preferred, many of them, to remain outside for the present, especially the rulers; the verb for joining he glosses as to cleave to like glue, and the people he takes as individuals among the populace, distinct from the rulers and hostile outsiders. Of the increase he notes that they were rather added than diminished as one might expect, the imperfect passive meaning that they kept on being added.

Cyril takes the whole passage as an illustration of the Spirit’s power: by the hands of the Apostles were many signs and wonders wrought among the people, and so great was the spiritual grace shed around them that, gentle as they were, they were the objects of dread, for of the rest durst no man join himself to them, but the people magnified them; multitudes were added of those who believed on the Lord, both of men and women; the streets were filled with the sick on their beds and couches, that as Peter passed by at least his shadow might overshadow some of them; and the multitude also of the cities round about came unto this holy Jerusalem, bringing sick folk and them that were vexed with unclean spirits, and they were healed every one in this power of the Holy Ghost.

debates: Who the rest were: Lightfoot confines them to the hundred and twenty, Ananias perhaps among them, so terrified by the fate of one of their own order that they dared not claim equality with the Twelve; Barnes calls that far-fetched and prefers the rich and the men of authority, giving four reasons; Ellicott takes them for the Pharisees and teachers who frequented the portico and sympathised without the courage to attach themselves; Clarke follows Calmet in making them the sects, none of which dared join a body that had adopted none of their opinions; Gill canvasses three readings and settles on men inside the church, ministers included.

Whether Peter’s shadow healed anyone: Barnes insists the writer neither says that it did nor that they were told to try it, and leaves the question to conjecture, contrasting the express statement about the handkerchiefs from Paul’s body; Henry thinks it plainly succeeded, like the touch of the hem of Christ’s garment, and finds in it the fulfilment of the promise of greater works.

Why Peter’s shadow rather than another apostle’s: Lightfoot raises the question none of the others raise, since the Twelve shared an equal power of miracles, and answers it twice, that the sick were carried out only when Peter was known to be passing, and that those who carried them may have known no other apostle by sight.
outliers: Ellicott dates the scene to winter on the ground that the eastward portico caught the morning sunlight and was then most frequented.

Calvin turns the awe that held outsiders back into a complaint against his own age, that there is a secret majesty in holy discipline which binds even the wicked, but that we have made ourselves despised along with the gospel by our profane liberty of evil living.

Henry denies that any healing virtue can be inferred for the relics of dead saints, since not one cure is recorded from the relics of Christ himself, as certainly there would have been had there been any such thing.
