Barnes draws the rule that cutting off unworthy members, however rich or honoured, increases a church’s numbers as well as its purity, since men will not trouble to enter a body that does not care to be pure.
themes: of the rest durst no man join

17.pericope_label: Then the high priest rose up, and all they that were with him, (which is the sect of the Sadducees,) and were filled with indignation, and laid their hands on the apostles, and put them in the common prison. But the angel of the Lord by night opened the prison doors, and brought them forth, and said, Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life. And when they heard that, they entered into the temple early in the morning, and taught. But the high priest came, and they that were with him, and called the council together, and all the senate of the children of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought

schools.summary: Gill takes the high priest to be Annas or rather Caiaphas, who, having heard what miracles were wrought by the apostles and what additions were made to them, rose up from his seat and went out of the sanhedrim in great haste and in much wrath and passion; the laying on of hands he understands of seizing and carrying them away, at least by their servants at their orders. The angel he calls a good angel, an elect angel, one of those ministering spirits sent to minister to the heirs of promise, one of those angels that excel in strength, as appears by what he did, though what particular angel it was he does not think material to know. The apostles, he says, were not delivered out of prison in order to go and secure themselves from danger, but to go about the work they were called to, to preach the Gospel in the temple, the place of worship and a proper place to meet with persons to preach to, being public and much resorted to; and there they were to stand and continue with courage and intrepidity, not fearing the reproach and wrath of men, seeing they had both Christ and truth on their side, and there to declare it to the people, the common people and multitude, even all that came to hear, since the Gospel is to be preached to all, the Spirit of God making it effectual to some and others being rendered inexcusable. Calvin observes that Luke has hitherto declared how the Church was wonderfully increased, magnificently furnished with divers gifts and excelling in miracles, and now begins to show that the fury of the wicked was kindled by these things so that they raged more violently afresh; whence we may gather with what blind fury and rage Satan drives them forward, when they are so little terrified with such evident power of God that they run headlong the more boldly and bend all their force, as it were, to overthrow the very heaven. As this great blindness is a horrible punishment of Almighty God, so it ought to teach all men to submit themselves betimes to God, lest they too, being taken with the spirit of giddiness, be broken while they run against the hand of God. Of the deliverance he says the Lord brought the apostles out of prison, not because he would rid them quite out of the hands of their enemies, for he suffered them afterwards to be brought back again and to be beaten with rods, but because he meant to declare by this miracle that they were in his hand and tuition, to the end he might maintain the credit of the gospel, partly that the Church might have another confirmation and partly that the wicked might be left without excuse; wherefore we must not hope always, nay we must not always desire, that God will deliver us from death, but must be content with this one thing, that our life is defended by his hand so far as is expedient. In using the ministry of an angel he does according to his common custom, since he testifies everywhere in the Scriptures that the angels are ministers of his goodness towards us; nor is that a vain speculation, for it is a profitable help for our infirmity that we should know not only that God cares for us but that the heavenly spirits watch for our safety, and it was no small pledge of God’s love that the creatures of all others most noble are appointed to have regard of our safety. The angel opens the prison in the night, he adds, because he would not work the miracle when the wicked might see him, although he would have it known by the event itself. The end of the deliverance he takes to be that they might employ themselves stoutly in preaching the gospel and provoke their enemies courageously until they died valiantly; for they were put to death at length when the hand of God ceased, after they had finished their course, but now the Lord opens the prison that they may be at liberty to fulfil their function. This is worth marking, he says, because we see many men who after they have escaped out of persecution afterwards keep silence, as if they had done their duty towards God, while others escape by denying Christ; but the Lord delivers his children, not that they may cease from the course they have begun, but rather that they may be the more zealous afterward. The apostles might have objected that it were better to keep silence for a time, since they could not speak one word without danger and were apprehended for one sermon only, so that the fury of their enemies would be the more inflamed if they made no end of speaking; but because they knew that they were to live and to die to the Lord, they do not refuse to do what the Lord commanded, and so we must always mark what function the Lord enjoins us, since many things will meet us which may discourage us unless, being content with the commandment of God alone, we do our duty and commit the success to him. The angel’s phrase he calls a singular commendation of the gospel, that it is a lively doctrine bringing salvation to men, since the righteousness of God is revealed in it and in it Christ offers himself with the sacrifice of his death, the Spirit of regeneration and the earnest of our adoption; and this is spoken expressly to the apostles that they may the more courageously enter all manner of combats for the gospel, hearing that they are ministers of eternal salvation. The demonstrative is added for the more certainty, as if the angel did point out life with his finger, since assuredly we need not seek the same far off when we have the word in our mouth and in our heart; though some had rather take it for these words, which Calvin does not reject, he thinks the former sense the better, for it was a new revelation of Christ wherein they had life present.

Henry observes that never did any good work go on with any hope of success but it met with opposition, since those bent to do mischief cannot be reconciled to those who make it their business to do good, and Satan, the destroyer of mankind, ever was and will be an adversary to those who are the benefactors of mankind; it would have been strange if the apostles had gone on thus teaching and healing and had had no check. Of the persecutors he notes that the high priest was the ringleader, Annas or Caiaphas, who saw his wealth and dignity, his power and tyranny, that is his all, at stake and inevitably lost if the spiritual and heavenly doctrine of Christ should prevail among the people; and that those most forward to join with him were the sect of the Sadducees, who had a particular enmity to the gospel of Christ because it confirmed and established the doctrine of the invisible world, the resurrection of the dead and the future state, which they denied. It is not strange, he adds, if men of no religion be bigoted in their opposition to true and pure religion. They were ill affected and exasperated to the last degree, and when they heard and saw what flocking there was to the apostles, and how considerable they were become, they rose up in a passion as men who could no longer bear it and were resolved to make head against it, being filled with indignation at the apostles for preaching the doctrine of Christ and curing the sick, and at the people for hearing them. Lightfoot says there is no necessity that the angel’s words should beget any difficulty, if we will observe that there is mention just before of the sect of the Sadducees, so that the words of this life are words that assert and prove this life, that is the resurrection, which the Sadducees deny; for the controversy was about the resurrection of Jesus.

Clarke observes that in this place, as in several others, the word rendered sect has no evil meaning in itself, being a word of distinction which may receive either a good or a bad colouring from the persons or opinions designated by it; it signifies a sect or party, whether good or bad, distinguished from any other, and comes from a verb meaning to choose, having anciently been applied to the different sects of the heathen philosophers, the members of each having chosen their own in preference to all the others. It has been applied among ecclesiastical writers in the same way, when a man chooses one party of Christians in preference to others to be his companions in the way of salvation, because he believes their creed and discipline more consistent with the oracles of God. The Church of Rome, he says, has thought proper to attach a very bad meaning to this innocent word and then to apply it to all those who can neither credit her transubstantiation, depend on her purgatory, nor worship her relics, a heretic in her acceptation being one who is not a papist and therefore out of the possibility of being saved; such persons should recollect that by a then persecuting brother Paul, all the apostles and the whole Church of Christ were termed the heresy of the Nazarenes, that it was after the way which the persecuting Jews called heresy that Paul worshipped the God of his fathers, that it was according to the strictest heresy in the Jewish Church that he lived before his conversion, and that the whole Church of Christ was termed this heresy by persons who intended no reproach but wished simply to distinguish the Christians from scribes, Pharisees and Sadducees. Heresy therefore in its first acceptation signifies simply a choice, and was afterwards applied to designate all those persons who made the same choice, so that it became synonymous with sect; in process of time it was applied to those professing Christianity who made in some cases a different choice as to some article of faith or form of worship from those which had obtained in that part of the Church with which they had been connected, and the majority from whom they thus separated spoke evil of them and treated them ill, because they presumed to choose for themselves on the foundation of the Holy Scriptures and would take nothing for the truth of God that was not accredited from heaven. The word for indignation he explains from a root meaning to be hot, signifying a vehement affection or disposition of the mind which, according to its object, is either good or bad, and says we need not be surprised that the Sadducees were filled with it, since the apostles proclaimed the resurrection of Christ and through it the general resurrection, diametrically opposed to their doctrine, they denying the possibility of a resurrection and believing neither in angel nor spirit nor in the existence of a spiritual world. The opening of the prison doors he says was done first to increase the confidence of the apostles by showing them that they were under the continual care of God, and secondly to show the Jewish rulers that they were fighting against him while persecuting his followers and attempting to prevent them from preaching the Gospel; it was another warning graciously given them, that they might repent and so escape the coming wrath. The angel’s phrase he takes for all the doctrines of eternal life founded on the word, death and resurrection of Christ, another periphrasis for the Gospel: go to the temple, the most public place, and speak to the people who come there to worship according to the law the whole doctrine of salvation from sin and death, showing that the law is fulfilled in the sacrifice of Jesus and that by his resurrection he has brought life and immortality to light. Of the assembly summoned in the morning he notes the council and the elders, or what we would call the aldermen, and confesses that how these differed from the presbytery, if they did differ, is not now known. Wesley glosses the phrase simply as these words of life, words which show the way to life everlasting.

Barnes takes the high priest to be probably Caiaphas, notes that it appears from this place that he belonged to the sect of the Sadducees, and that those with him were the Sadducean portion of the sanhedrim, perhaps at this time so strong a majority as to control its decisions. The word translated sect, he says, is that from which we have derived our word heresy; it means simply sect or party and is not used in a bad sense as implying reproach or even error, the idea we attach to it of error and of denying fundamental doctrines being one that does not occur in the New Testament. The main doctrine of the Sadducees was the denial of the resurrection of the dead, and the reason they were opposed to the apostles rather than the Pharisees was that the apostles dwelt much on the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, which if true completely overthrew their doctrine, every convert diminishing their numbers and influence and establishing the Pharisees in their belief. So long, therefore, as the effect of the apostles’ labours was to establish one of the main doctrines of the Pharisees and to confute the Sadducees, the Pharisees would either favour them or be silent, while the Sadducees would be enraged; for one sect will often see with composure the progress of another that it really hates, if it will humble a rival, and even opposition to the gospel will sometimes be silent provided the spread of religion will humble those against whom we are opposed. The word for indignation he glosses as zeal, denoting any kind of fervour or warmth and applicable to any violent affection of the mind, whether envy, wrath, zeal or love, and here probably including envy and wrath: they were envious at the success of the apostles and at the accession of strength to the Pharisees, and indignant that their own authority was so little regarded. The common prison he explains as the public prison, or the prison for the keeping of common and notorious offenders. The angel he says denotes not any particular angel but simply an angel, the article not being used in the original, and the case was evidently a miracle, the design of which may have been to reprove the Jewish rulers and convince them of their guilt in resisting the gospel, to convince the apostles more firmly of the divine protection and approbation, to encourage them in their work, and to give the people a new and impressive proof of the truth of the message they bore; for that they were imprisoned was known to the people, and that they were made as secure as possible was also known, so that when next morning, before they could have been tried or acquitted, they were found again in the temple delivering the same message, it was a new and striking proof that they were sent by God. The temple he calls a public and conspicuous place, in which their boldness would be most strikingly exhibited; and the words of this life he takes as all the doctrines pertaining to the eternal life which they taught through the resurrection and life of Jesus, life being used sometimes for the whole of religion as opposed to the spiritual death of sin. Their deliverance from prison, he adds, was not that they might be idle and escape to a place of safety, but that they might at once engage in the toils and perils they had just encountered; God delivers us from danger sometimes that we may plunge into new dangers, preserves us from calamity that we may be tried in some new furnace of affliction, and calls us to encounter trials simply because he demands it and as an expression of gratitude for his gracious interposition. The early morning he renders as the break of day, and the council as the sanhedrim, called together clearly for the purpose of trying the apostles for disregarding their commandment; the senate he takes as probably not a part of the sanhedrim but men of age and experience, elsewhere called elders of the Jews, present for the sake of counsel and advice in a case of emergency. Ellicott takes the high priest to be, as before, Annas or Caiaphas, and calls the statement that they were of the sect of the Sadducees, of which this is the only distinct record, of immense importance as throwing light on the course of action taken by the upper class of priests both during our Lord’s ministry and in the history of this book: from the time of the teaching about the resurrection they must have felt that his doctrine was diametrically opposed to theirs, they made one attempt to turn it into ridicule and were baffled, and the raising of Lazarus mingled a dogmatic antagonism with the counsels of political expediency, so that the prominence of the Resurrection of Jesus in the teaching of the Apostles now made the Sadducean high priests their most determined opponents; the Pharisees, less exposed now to the condemnation our Lord had passed on their unreality, were drawing off into a position at first of declared neutrality, then of secret sympathy, then in many cases of professed adherence. The word for indignation he says is elsewhere rendered zeal or envy, and both meanings were probably applicable, there being zeal against the doctrine and envy of the popularity of the Apostles. The common prison he takes as the same word for ward used earlier, the addition of common or public perhaps indicating a greater severity of treatment, since they were not merely kept in custody but dealt with as common criminals, compelled to herd with ruffians and robbers and murderers. The angel he renders better as an angel, the fact being obviously recorded as supernatural; those who do not accept that view and yet wish to maintain the general historical character of the narrative, he notes, are driven to the hypothesis that the angel was some jealous and courageous disciple, and that the Apostle in the darkness of the night and the excitement of his liberation ascribed his rescue to an angel. It has sometimes been urged, he adds, with something of a sneer, what was the use of such a deliverance when the Apostles were arrested again on the very next day; and the answer is not far to seek, since the marvellous deliverance was a sign not without its influence on the subsequent decision of the Council and on the courage of the Apostles, and it was no small boon for them to be delivered even for a few hours from the vile companionship to which they had been condemned. The demonstrative in the angel’s phrase he calls significant, the life in Christ which the Apostles preach being that eternal life which consists in knowing God and in which the angels are sharers. The morning he places probably at daybreak, when the worshippers would be going up to the Temple for their early devotions, or, though less probably, at the third hour, the time of the morning sacrifice; those with the high priest he takes for the same body named earlier, who seem to have acted as a kind of cabinet or committee; and the senate he says literally means the assembly of old men or elders, here distinguished from the Sanhedrin, which itself included elders in the official sense, and probably a body of assessors, how chosen we do not know, specially qualified by age and experience and called in on special occasions. Robertson renders the clause literally as the existing sect of the Sadducees, notes that the word means a choosing, then an opinion chosen or tenet, then parties or factions, and that it is applied here to the Sadducees, elsewhere to the Pharisees and to the Christians; already Luke has stated that the Sadducees started the persecution of Peter and John, and now it is extended to the apostles as a whole since Christianity has spread more rapidly in Jerusalem than before. The word for jealousy he traces to a verb meaning to boil, whence our zeal, and says that in itself it means only warmth or ardour, but that for a bad cause or from a bad motive jealousy, envy and rivalry result. The place of confinement he calls the public prison, adding that any prison is bad enough, and that it is called the guardhouse in the next verse. The command to stand he parses as an ingressive aorist participle, a bold and pictorial command; and the words of this life he says are not just a Hebraism for all these words of life, but probably mean this life which the Sadducees deny and of which the angel is now speaking, this eternal life. The dawn he traces to a verb meaning to stir up, an old word occurring in the New Testament only three times, and observes that the temple doors would be open for early worshippers and traffickers; the verb of teaching he parses as an imperfect, they began to teach, and the senate he derives from the word for an old man, just as the Latin senate is from the word for old.

Chrysostom describes the high priest and his party as roused and excited at the things taking place, assaulting the apostles now more vigorously and putting them in the common prison, but not bringing them at once to trial because they expected them to be softened down. The deliverance, he says, was both for the encouragement of the disciples and for the benefit and instruction of the others; and he observes how the proceeding in the present instance is just the same as in what Christ himself did, since in his miracles, though he does not let men see them in the act of being wrought, he furnishes the means whereby they may be apprised of the things wrought: thus in his Resurrection he did not let them see how he rose, and in the water made wine the guests do not see it done, for they have been drinking much, and the discernment he leaves to others. Just so in the present case they do not see the apostles in the act of being brought forth, but the proofs from which they might gather what had been done they do see. And it was by night that the Angel put them forth, which Chrysostom explains by saying that in this way they were more believed than they would have been in the other, since people would not even have had occasion to put the question, and would not in some other way have believed; so it was in the old times in the case of Nebuchadnezzar, who saw the three praising God in the furnace and then indeed was put in amazement. Whereas the priests ought as their first question to have asked how they came out, instead of this, as if nothing had happened, they ask whether they had not been straitly charged not to speak. By report of others they are apprised of all the circumstances: they see the prison remaining closed with safety and the guards standing before the doors, a twofold security, as was the case at the sepulchre, where was both the seal and the men to watch. See how they fought against God, he exclaims: was this of man’s doing? Who led them forth when the doors were shut, and how came they out with the keepers standing before the door? Here are men whom neither prison nor bonds nor closed doors had been able to keep in, and yet they expect to overpower them, such is their childish folly; and their own officers come and confess what has taken place, as if on purpose to debar them from all show of reason. There is miracle upon miracle, differing in kind, some wrought by the apostles and others upon them, and these more illustrious than the others.

debates: What the words of this life mean: Lightfoot ties the phrase directly to the resurrection which the Sadducees deny, since that was the whole controversy, and Robertson agrees that this life is the one they denied; Ellicott makes it the eternal life which consists in knowing God and in which the angels themselves are sharers; Calvin takes the demonstrative for a gesture of certainty, as though the angel pointed at life with his finger, adding that we need not seek far for what is already in our mouth and heart.

Whether the deliverance served any purpose, given the re-arrest: Ellicott states the sneer plainly and answers it twice, that the sign told on the Council’s decision and on the apostles’ courage, and that release even for a few hours from that companionship was no small boon; Barnes lists four ends it served; Calvin denies that deliverance from death is what we should hope for at all, only that our life is defended so far as is expedient.

What the word rendered sect implies: Barnes and Robertson both insist it carries no reproach in the New Testament and means simply a party or a thing chosen; Clarke agrees and turns it into a long protest against the Roman use of heretic; Ellicott passes over the word and treats the fact of Sadducean high priests as the key to the whole history.
outliers: Barnes observes that one sect will often watch with composure the growth of another it hates, if that growth humbles a rival, and that opposition to the gospel will sometimes fall silent on the same terms.

Chrysostom argues that Christ never let men see a miracle in the act of being wrought but always left the proofs, instancing the Resurrection and the water made wine, and compares the shut doors and posted guards to the seal and the watch at the sepulchre.
Calvin finds a pledge of God’s love in the choice of instrument, that the noblest of creatures are appointed to have regard of our safety.
Barnes remarks that God delivers us from danger sometimes in order that we may plunge into new dangers, and preserves us from one calamity to try us in another furnace.

22.pericope_label: But when the officers came, and found them not in the prison, they returned, and told, saying, The prison truly found we shut with all safety, and the keepers standing without before the doors: but when we had opened, we found no man within. Now when the high priest and the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these things, they doubted of them whereunto this would grow. Then came one and told them, saying, Behold, the men whom ye put in prison are standing in the temple, and teaching the people. Then went the captain with the officers, and brought them without violence: for they feared the people, lest they should have been stoned

schools.summary: Gill notes that the Arabic version adds the words to it, that is to the prison, and describes the prison as locked, barred and bolted. On the alarm of the rulers he observes that most copies read the priests rather than the high priest, while the Complutensian edition reads the high priest, who is certainly designed since he is distinguished from the chief priests afterwards mentioned, and that the Vulgate, Syriac and Ethiopic versions and the Alexandrian copy leave the word out. Of the man who brought word he says that who he was is of no consequence to know, but that it can hardly be thought he was one of the number of the disciples, or a member of the church, or a professor of the Christian religion, but rather an enemy, and one that sought his own interest and to obtain the favour and affection of the chief priests and elders, and therefore very officiously came to them and reported. The captain who went to fetch them he identifies as the captain of the temple, who had command of it, attended by the officers and servants of the chief priests, the same who had been sent to the prison before.

Henry observes that we are not told what the apostles preached to the people, though no doubt it was according to the direction of the angel, the words of this life, but that what passed between them and the council is recorded, since in their sufferings there appeared more of a divine power and energy than even in their preaching. To the question why, if God designed this second seizure, they were rescued from the first imprisonment at all, he answers that the rescue was designed to humble the pride and check the fury of their persecutors, and that now God would show that they were discharged not because they feared a trial, since they were ready to surrender themselves and to make their appearance before the greatest of their enemies. They brought them without violence, he says, with all the respect and tenderness that could be, not pulling them out of the pulpit nor binding them nor dragging them along, but accosting them respectfully; and one would think they had reason to do so, in reverence to the temple, that holy place, and for fear of the apostles, lest they should strike them as they did Ananias, or call for fire from heaven upon them as Elias did; but all that restrained their violence was their fear of the people, who had such a veneration for the apostles that they would have stoned the officers if they had offered them any abuse. Yet they brought them, he adds, to those whom they knew to be violent against them and resolved to take violent courses with them, setting them before the council as delinquents; and thus the powers that should have been a terror to evil works and workers became so to the good.

Clarke observes that all the doors were properly bolted and the keepers at their post, and that it appears the officers were alone in possession of the keys; how much, he asks, must this have increased their astonishment when they found that the doors were not broken open, the guards properly posted, and everything as they had left it, for they themselves had put the apostles in prison, and yet when they had opened there was no man within. Of the rulers he says they did not know what to think of the apostles, whether they had saved themselves by magic or whether they were delivered by a real miracle, and were at a loss to tell what the issue of these things would be. While they were in that perplexity, he continues, a messenger surprised them with the information that the very men whom they had imprisoned the preceding night were standing in the temple and teaching the people; and on receiving this information proper officers were sent to seize and bring them before the council. The officers, on reaching the temple, found the multitude gladly receiving the doctrine of the apostles and so intent on hearing all the words of this life that they were afraid to show any hostility, lest the people should stone them; we may therefore conclude, he says, that the officers entreated them to accompany them to the council, and that the apostles felt it their duty to obey every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake, and so cheerfully went with them, trusting in the Lord their God. Wesley suggests that the angel had probably shut the doors again, and says of the rulers that they were even at their wits’ end, adding that the world, in persecuting the children of God, entangle themselves in numberless difficulties.

Barnes says the prison had not been broken open, so that there was clear proof that the apostles had been delivered by the interposition of God, nor could they have been released by the guard, for these were keeping watch as if unconscious that anything had happened, and the officers had the only means of entering the prison. The word rendered doubted he says denotes that state of anxiety which arises when a man has lost his way, or when he does not know what to do to escape from a difficulty, and the following clause asks what would be the result or end of these events; for their authority was disregarded, God had opposed them by a miracle, the doctrines of the apostles were gaining ground, and their efforts to oppose them had been in vain. They need not have doubted, he adds, but sinners are not disposed to be convinced of the truth of religion. Of the arrest he says the apostles were taken not by force nor by binding them, since the command of the sanhedrim was sufficient to secure their presence, as they did not intend to refuse to answer for any alleged violation of the laws; and besides, their going before the council would give them another noble opportunity to bear witness to the truth of the gospel. Christians, he concludes, when charged with a violation of the laws of the land, should not refuse to answer, since it is a part of our religion to yield obedience to all the just laws of the land and to evince respect for all that are in authority. The people were favourable to the apostles, and if violence had been attempted the consequence would have been a tumult and bloodshed; in this way also the apostles showed that they were not disposed to excite tumult, since opposition by them would have excited commotion, and though they would have been rescued they resolved to show that they were not obstinate or rebellious but disposed, so far as it could be done with a clear conscience, to yield obedience to the laws of the land. Ellicott prefers the reading high priest, observing that the use of the bare word priest to mean the high priest has no parallel in the New Testament and that the word is omitted by many of the best manuscripts, and identifies the captain of the temple as the commander of the Levite sentinels. The rulers’ perplexity he renders literally as what it might become, or possibly what it might be, and remarks that they do not seem to have recognised at once the supernatural character of what had taken place, and may have conjectured that the Apostles had by some human help effected their escape. The scene of the arrest he says recalls the sending of the officers in the Gospel, but that here the Apostles set the example of unresisting acquiescence, even though the tide of feeling in their favour was so strong that they might easily have raised a tumult; the signs that had recently been wrought, and perhaps also the lavish distribution of alms and the ideal communism of the disciples, were all likely, till counteracted by stronger influences, to secure popular favour. Robertson glosses the officers as under-rowers, literally, the servants who executed the orders of the Sanhedrin, parses the participle for the shut prison as a perfect passive meaning shut tight, and calls the sentinels standing at the doors a graphic picture. The verb of perplexity he parses as an imperfect used by Luke alone in the New Testament, so that they continued puzzled, and renders the indirect question more exactly as, as to what this would become, a second aorist middle optative in the conclusion of a condition of the fourth class, the unexpressed condition being that the thing should be allowed to go on; if they had only known, he exclaims, how this grain of mustard seed would grow into the greatest tree on earth, and how dwarfed the tree of Judaism would be beside it. The bringing he parses as an imperfect, was bringing or leading, slowly no doubt and solemnly, and the fear as an imperfect middle, they kept on fearing; the clause about stoning he takes as a negative purpose attached probably to the words about violence, so that they handled the apostles gently for fear of being stoned themselves by the people.

debates: What the rulers made of the escape: Barnes holds the proof clear and says they need not have doubted, adding that sinners are simply not disposed to be convinced of the truth of religion; Clarke leaves them genuinely undecided whether the apostles had saved themselves by magic or been delivered by a real miracle; Ellicott thinks they did not recognise anything supernatural at all and probably supposed some human help.

Why the officers used no violence: Henry allows that reverence for the temple, or a fear of being struck like Ananias or scorched like the mockers of Elias, might have restrained them, but concludes that nothing did so except fear of the people; Robertson agrees flatly that they were afraid of being stoned themselves; Barnes and Ellicott turn the credit the other way, to the apostles, who neither resisted nor raised the tumult that lay ready to hand.

Who brought the news: Gill holds it hardly possible that a disciple or professor of the religion did so, and guesses an enemy currying favour with the chief priests; Clarke leaves the messenger anonymous and only marks the surprise of the news arriving while the council sat baffled.
outliers: Robertson exclaims that the council little knew how that grain of mustard seed would grow into the greatest tree on earth, and how dwarfed the tree of Judaism would look beside it.
Wesley remarks that the world, in persecuting the children of God, entangles itself in numberless difficulties.
Barnes draws from the peaceable arrest a rule for Christians charged with breaking the laws of the land, that they should not refuse to answer but yield obedience to every just law.
Henry answers the question why the apostles were freed at night only to be taken in the morning, that it humbled the pride of their persecutors and showed the discharge was no flight from trial.

27.pericope_label: And when they had brought them, they set them before the council: and the high priest asked them, saying, Did not we straitly command you that ye should not teach in this name? and, behold, ye have filled Jerusalem with your doctrine, and intend to bring this man’s blood upon us. Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree. Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins. And we are his witnesses of these things; and so is also the Holy Ghost, whom God hath given to them that obey him

schools.summary: Gill notes that the apostles were brought from the temple to the place where the sanhedrim sat, which by this seems to have been not in the room Gazith nor in the shops, both of which were in the temple, but in some part of the city; and he glosses the charge as strict orders given with severe threatenings. Peter, he says, began as the mouth of the apostles, being the eldest man and very bold and zealous, and the rest joined with him. The raising up of Jesus he refers not to the resurrection, though that was true, but to God’s calling him to the work and office of a Saviour, investing him with that office and sending him to perform the work, so that it refers rather to the incarnation, in consequence of the ancient council and covenant of grace; and this the apostles attribute to the Father under the character of the God of their fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to show that they did not bring in and worship any strange God, nor introduce any novel doctrine, nor speak of any other Saviour than he whom the God of their fathers had appointed and whom they looked for. The exaltation he takes as being not at his right hand, though Christ is exalted to it and set down at it, but with or by his right hand, that is by his power; for being raised from the dead he was exalted to the highest heavens and placed in human nature at the right hand of God, on the same throne with him, crowned with glory and honour, having a name above every name and all authority in heaven and earth given him. Calvin observes that the chief priest lays two crimes to the charge of the apostles, accusing them of contumacy because they did not obey the decree of the council, and in the second member betraying an evil conscience, or at least showing that he handled a private business rather than a public cause, since he complains that the apostles will cause the priests and scribes to be hated for the death of Christ; behold therefore, he says, what it is that nettles them, that they fear the revenge and punishment of a wicked murder. He pretends doctrine at the first, but we may gather from the end that he was not so careful for doctrine; meanwhile he accuses the apostles of sedition, taking for granted what most men did grant, that Christ was put to death justly. The principal point of the accusation is that they did not obey the commandment of the priests, and Calvin turns this against the tyranny of office: the chief priest does not consider what his duty is towards God and the Church but abuses his authority as if it were under no laws, as the Pope deals with us at this day, catching at the sentence that he who despises you despises me and concluding that we rebel against God; but if he will be heard as the ambassador of Christ he must speak out of the mouth of Christ. The very form of speech, with a commandment have we commanded, proves how carelessly spiritual tyrants who usurp an authority not subject to the word of God grant themselves liberty to attempt whatever pleases them. Of the answer he says the sum is that it is lawful for the apostles, nay they ought, to prefer God before men: God commands them to bear witness of Christ, therefore it is in vain to command them to keep silence. But he has declared before when this sentence takes place, since God sets men over us in such sort that he keeps his own authority safe and sound, so that we must obey rulers so far that the commandment of God be not broken. Where power is lawfully used it is out of season to make comparison between God and man; if a faithful pastor command or forbid out of the Word of God it is in vain for stubborn men to object that we ought to obey God, for God will be heard by man, and man is nothing else but an instrument of God; if a magistrate do his duty as he ought, a man shall in vain say that he is contrary to God, seeing he dissents in nothing, and rather the contrary rule is in force, that we must obey God’s ministers and officers if we will obey him. But so soon as rulers lead us away from the obedience of God, because they strive against God with sacrilegious boldness, their pride must be abated that God may be above all in authority, and then all smokes of honour vanish away; for God does not vouchsafe to bestow honourable titles upon men to the end they may darken his glory. If a father, not content with his own estate, essay to take from God the chief honour of a father, he is nothing else but a man; if a king or ruler or magistrate become so lofty that he diminishes the honour and authority of God, he is but a man; and we must think the same of pastors, for he who goes beyond his bounds in his office sets himself against God and must be despoiled of his honour, lest under a visor he deceive. The office of a pastor is very excellent and the authority of the Church is great, yet so that no part of God’s power and Christ’s mastership be diminished; whence we may easily gather that the pride of the Pope is ridiculous, who, treading under foot the whole kingdom of Christ and setting himself openly against God, will yet lie hid under the name of Christ. On the exaltation he says the right hand is taken for his power, and that the metaphor is not the same as elsewhere when Christ is said to be lifted up unto the right hand of the Father, the meaning here being that Christ, slain by the hand of men, was lifted up on high by the power of God that he might bear rule over angels and men; and this seems secretly set against all the enterprises of Satan and the world, as if to say that they shall have no good success, because they shall never climb so high as to hinder the hand of God. The end is added also, that he may be a captain and Saviour, since so often as God put his people in hope of salvation he was wont to promise a prince or a king by whose hand he would restore all things; the sum is that Christ is placed in the highest degree of honour that he may govern the people of God, and not that only but that he may show himself the author of salvation, and they show how he reigns to save, namely when he brings his own to repentance and reconciles them to God through the remission of sins, in which two things the sum of the gospel is contained.

Clarke renders the opening charge from the Hebraism as, with commanding did we not command you, and calls it another proof of the accuracy and fidelity of Luke, who seems always to give every man’s speech as he delivered it, not the substance but the very words. The name he explains as that of Jesus as the Christ or Messiah, his saving name and the doctrines connected with it being the only theme and substance of their discourses; and the complaint about the blood he paraphrases as, you speak of him to the people in such a way as to persuade them that we have crucified an innocent man, and that we must on that account fall victims to the divine vengeance or to the fury of the people whom you are exciting to sedition against us. The apostles’ answer he refers to the same words given before, founded on the same reason, which still stood good: we have received our commission from God, and dare not lay it down at the desire or command of men. The naming of the God of the fathers he thinks well introduced, that the council might at once see the apostles preached no strange God, and that he who so highly honoured the patriarchs, Moses and the prophets had yet more highly honoured Jesus Christ by raising him from the dead, seating him at his right hand, and proclaiming him the only giver of salvation and of the repentance which leads to it; and again, he notes, they charge them with the murder of Christ. The exaltation he explains as by a supereminent display of almighty power, for so the right hand of God often means, God having raised him from the dead and raised his human nature to the throne of his glory, and he records a manuscript which reads to glory instead of with the right hand. The Prince he glosses as the leader or director in the way, and the Saviour as a deliverer or preserver, the two words Jesus and Saviour being nearly of the same import, since he alone delivers from sin, death and hell. Forgiveness he takes as the taking away of sins, not to be restrained to the mere act of justification but implying the removal of sin whether its power, guilt or impurity be considered, since through Jesus we have the destruction of the power, the pardon of the guilt and the cleansing from the pollution of sin. And was Jesus Christ exalted a Prince and a Saviour to give repentance and remission of sins to Israel, he asks; then none need despair, for if such as were now before the apostles could be saved, then the salvation of the very worst of transgressors is gloriously possible, since he tasted death for every man and prayed for his murderers. Wesley sees the poor cunning of the enemies of the Gospel, who make laws and interdicts at their pleasure which those who obey God cannot but break, and then take occasion thereby to censure and punish the innocent as guilty; and he calls the complaint about the blood an artful and invidious word, since the apostles did not desire to accuse any man but simply declared the naked truth. He notes that Peter now does not give them the titles of honour which he did before but enters directly upon the subject and justifies what he had done, this being as it were a continuation of that earlier discourse but with an increase of severity.

Barnes glosses the charge as commanding with a threat, and takes the complaint that they had filled Jerusalem as, though not so designed, an honourable tribute to the zeal and fidelity of the apostles; when Christians are arraigned or persecuted, he says, it is well if the only charge their enemies can bring is that they have been distinguished for zeal and success in propagating their religion. To bring one’s blood upon another he explains as a phrase denoting to hold or prove him guilty of murdering the innocent, so that the rulers charge the apostles with designing to prove that they had put Jesus to death when he was innocent, to convince the people of this and thus enrage them against the sanhedrim, and to prove that they were exposed to the divine vengeance for having put the Messiah to death. That the apostles did intend to charge them with murder is clear, he grants, but it is observable that on this occasion they had said nothing of it, and further that they did not charge it on them except in their presence, taking no pains to spread it among the people; their consciences were not at ease, and the remembrance of the death of Jesus would occur to them at the sight of the apostles. The answer he refers to the earlier hearing. The raising up he refers to the resurrection, and the hanging on a tree to the cross; and he sums up the defence, that Peter begins with the great principle which they could not gainsay, that God ought to be obeyed rather than man, then states that they were convinced God had raised up Jesus, and that as they had such decisive evidence and were commanded to be witnesses of it, they were not at liberty to be silent. The remark that God had raised up Jesus whom they had slain does not seem to have been made to irritate them, he adds, but mainly to identify the person raised, and it was also a confirmation of the truth and reality of the miracle, since of his death they had no doubt, having been at pains to certify it; yet Peter did not shrink from charging on them their guilt, nor take any pains to soften the charge that they had murdered their own Messiah. Of the exaltation he says the title Prince means that Christ is actually in the exercise of the office at the right hand of his Father, denoting the dominion and power needful to give repentance and pardon; repentance he takes as equivalent to reformation and a change of life, and Israel as properly denoting the Jews, though the office was not confined to them, the reasons for the particular mention being that the Messiah was long promised to that people and that Peter was addressing Jews. If it be asked in what sense the Lord Jesus gives repentance, or how his exaltation is connected with it, he answers in four ways: that his exaltation is evidence that his work was accepted, so that a foundation is laid by which repentance may be connected with pardon, since without some way of forgiveness sorrow for sin would be of no value; that he is entrusted with all power in heaven and earth with reference to applying his work to men; that his exaltation is immediately connected with the bestowing of the Holy Spirit, by whose influence men are brought to repentance; and that in this state of exaltation he has power over all things that can affect the mind, sending his ministers and directing the events of sickness or health, disappointment or prosperity, that will influence the heart, and being able to recall the sins of the past life and refresh the memory so as to overwhelm the soul with the consciousness of guilt. It was proper, he argues, that the power of pardon should be lodged with the same Being that has the power of producing repentance, since the one appropriately follows the other and both are parts of the same great work; and from this he infers that Jesus Christ is divine, since it is a dictate both of natural religion and of the Bible that none can forgive sins against God but God himself, and yet Christ exercised this power on earth and exercises it still in heaven. He closes with the encouragement that Christ has power to pardon the greatest offender, since even his murderers he could pardon, so that no sinner need fear that he who is a Prince and a Saviour at the right hand of God is unable to pardon every sin. Ellicott notes that the Greek of the opening charge presents the same Hebrew idiom as at the earlier hearing and suggests again that it is a translation of the Aramaic actually spoken, and prefers teaching to doctrine, both to keep up the connection with the previous clause and because the word is taken in its wider sense and not in the modern sense of a formulated opinion. In the phrase about the blood he finds a touch partly of scorn and partly, it may be, of fear, in the careful avoidance of the name of Jesus, as before in this name; the words Peter had uttered gave some colour to the conscience-stricken priests for the charge, but it was a strange complaint from those who had stirred up the people to cry that his blood should be on them and on their children. The apostles’ answer he takes as an assertion of the same general law of duty as before, though the command of the angel had given it a new significance, and he notes that the whole company of the Twelve were now the objects of attack and all accept Peter as their spokesman. The phrase about hanging on a tree he traces to the Greek version of Deuteronomy, where it is used in a wider sense including analogous forms of punishment such as hanging or impaling, and notes that it meets us again in Peter’s speech to Cornelius. Of the exaltation he observes that Peter uses a word which, while it does not occur as applied to our Lord in the first three Gospels, meets us so applied in the fourth, and had also been used of the righteous sufferer in the Greek Old Testament and was afterwards used of the ascended Christ by Paul; and in the giving of repentance he notes the essential unity of the teaching of the Apostles with that of the Baptist, the beginning and the end being the same in each, what was characteristic of the new teaching being a fuller revelation of the way in which forgiveness had been obtained, of the spiritual gifts that followed, and of the society which was to bear witness of both. Robertson parses the setting of them before the council as a transitive first aorist, and the doubled charge as the Hebrew idiom common in the Greek Old Testament, with charging we charged, somewhat like the cognate accusative; he notes that the Sanhedrin had gladly taken the blood of Christ upon their heads and their children before Pilate, and calls the phrase this man a contemptuous slur and refusal to name Jesus, as in the Talmud later. The necessity in the answer he calls moral, leaving them no choice, and the verb of obeying he derives from words meaning to obey a ruler, a word used in the New Testament only by Luke and Paul. The verb for slaying he glosses as an old one meaning to take in hand, to manage, to lay hands on or manhandle, and the hanging upon a tree he refers, like Ellicott, to the curse pronounced in Deuteronomy on everyone who hangs upon a tree, as Paul also applies it. The exaltation he sets in contrast with their murder of Christ, noting that Peter repeats his charges with increased boldness, and allows the phrase about the right hand to be instrumental, locative or dative.

Cyril recalls the scene in brief as one of the Spirit’s works: after the Twelve Apostles had been cast into prison by the chief priests for preaching Christ, and had been marvellously delivered from it at night by an Angel, they were brought before them in the judgment hall.

debates: How far obedience to rulers reaches: Calvin states the rule and its limits at length, that the comparison between God and man arises only where there is contrariety, that a faithful pastor or magistrate commanding lawfully is not to be resisted by an appeal to God, since God chooses to be heard through men, but that rulers who lead us away from obedience to God lose their titles altogether — father, king and pastor alike becoming only men; Clarke and Barnes simply refer the answer back to the earlier hearing, and Robertson says moral necessity left the apostles no choice.

What the raising up of Jesus means: Gill refers it not to the resurrection but to God’s calling and sending of Christ to the office of a Saviour, in consequence of the ancient covenant; Barnes and Clarke both refer it to the resurrection, Barnes adding that the mention of the killing serves to identify the person raised and to confirm the reality of the death.

What the exaltation with the right hand means: Gill, Calvin and Robertson take the phrase for the power by which Christ was raised rather than the place at God’s side, Calvin adding that it is set against every enterprise of Satan, which can never climb high enough to hinder the hand of God; Ellicott notes instead that the verb is the one the fourth Gospel uses of the lifting up on the cross and Paul of the glory that followed.
outliers: Barnes turns the accusation into a compliment, since it is well if the only charge an enemy can bring against Christians is zeal and success in spreading their religion.

Calvin turns the priest’s doubled command into a case against spiritual tyranny, that men who usurp an authority not subject to the word of God grant themselves liberty to attempt whatever pleases them.
Clarke draws the pastoral inference that if such men as then stood before the apostles could be saved, none need despair, since Christ tasted death for every man and prayed for his own murderers.
Robertson calls the phrase this man a contemptuous slur and a refusal to pronounce the name of Jesus, as in the later rabbinic writings.
themes: did not we straitly command you
we ought to obey God rather than men

33.pericope_label: When they heard that, they were cut to the heart, and took counsel to slay them. Then stood there up one in the council, a Pharisee, named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people, and commanded to put the apostles forth a little space; and said unto them, Ye men of Israel, take heed to yourselves what ye intend to do as touching these men

schools.summary: Gill takes the occasion of the rage to be the apostles’ defence, in which they still insisted that the council had been the crucifiers of Christ and yet that he was raised from the dead and exalted in heaven and was a spiritual Saviour of men. Of the man who rose he notes that he was one of the members of the sanhedrim which the high priest had called together, and that it seems to have been the custom that though they usually sat, yet when anyone had anything to say or made a speech he rose up from his seat. Calvin says the priests ought to have been thoroughly moved though they had had hearts of iron, but instead they burst with rage; whence we gather that no reasons can prevail with the reprobate to bring them to the obedience of Christ, for unless God speak within, the outward doctrine can do nothing but beat the ears. The apostles were able so to overcome their enemies that they should not have had one word to say, but their fury was so untamed and unbridled that they rather go mad. Yet we must therewith note the force of the word, he adds, because although the reprobate are not thereby changed so as to become better, it pierces into their hearts so that it urges their consciences; thence springs their fury, because they feel themselves urged by their judge. They would gladly mock all the gospel, and attempt whatever they can that they may count it as nothing, but there is in it a certain hidden majesty which with a strong hand dispels all their delights; and chiefly when they are cited by the sound of the trumpet to appear before the judgment-seat of God, then appears their madness and fury.

Lightfoot identifies the speaker as Rabban Gamaliel the First, commonly and by way of distinction called Rabban Gamaliel the Old, president of the council after his own father Rabban Simeon, who was the son of Hillel. He was Paul’s master, he says, and the thirty-fifth receiver of the traditions, and upon this account might not improperly be termed a doctor of the law, because he was one that kept and handed down the Cabbala received from Mount Sinai, though Rabbins of an inferior degree enjoyed the same title also. He died eighteen years before the destruction of Jerusalem, his son Simeon succeeding him in the chair, who perished in the ruins of the city. Whereas he does in some measure apologise for the apostles, Lightfoot allows, one might believe that he favoured Christianity; but he died a Pharisee, and if he was not the author, yet he approved and recommended the prayer entitled a prayer against the heretics, of which Samuel the Little was the author, and whom they meant by heretics is easy enough to see. Henry sees a providence behind the intervention: the Lord still has all hearts in his hands, and sometimes directs the prudence of the worldly wise so as to restrain the persecutors; common sense tells us to be cautious, while experience and observation show that the success of frauds in matters of religion has been very short.

Clarke renders the phrase literally as, they were sawn through, from the words for through and to saw, and says they were stung to the heart not with compunction nor remorse but with spite, malice and revenge; for having the murder of Christ thus brought home to their consciences, in the first feelings of their malice and revenge they thought of destroying the persons who had witnessed their nefarious conduct. Of Gamaliel he quotes Lightfoot’s account entire, that this was Rabban Gamaliel the first, commonly by way of distinction called Rabban Gamaliel the elder, president of the council after the death of his own father Rabban Simeon, who was the son of Hillel; that he was Paul’s master and the thirty-fifth receiver of the traditions, and on this account might not improperly be termed a doctor of the law, because he was one that kept and handed down the Cabala received from Mount Sinai; and that he died eighteen years before the destruction of Jerusalem, his son Simeon succeeding him in the chair and perishing in the ruins of the city. Though probably no favourer of Christianity, Clarke adds, yet for a Pharisee he seems to have possessed a more liberal mind than most of his brethren, and the advice he was about to give was at once humane, sensible, candid and enlightened. Wesley passes over the scene without particular comment.

Barnes explains that what they heard was Peter’s charge that they were guilty of murder, that Jesus was raised up and that he still lived as the Messiah. The word rendered cut to the heart, he says, properly denotes to cut with a saw, and as applied to the mind it means to be agitated with rage and indignation, as if wrath should seize upon the mind as a saw does upon wood and tear it violently; it is commonly used in connection with the heart, and means that the heart is violently agitated and rent with rage, and it is not used elsewhere in the New Testament except of the scene after Stephen’s speech. The reasons for the indignation were doubtless that the apostles had disregarded their command, that they charged them with murder, and that they affirmed the doctrine of the resurrection of Jesus and so tended to overthrow the sect of the Sadducees; and he adds the general remark that the effect of the doctrines of the gospel is often to make men enraged. The phrase for taking counsel denotes commonly to will, then to deliberate, and sometimes to decree or determine, and it doubtless implies here that their minds were made up, but probably the formal decree was not passed to put the apostles to death. Of the speaker he notes that he rose, as is usual in deliberative assemblies, to speak, and that he was a Pharisee, whereas the high priest and those most active in opposing the apostles were Sadducees, the Pharisees being opposed to them particularly on the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead which the apostles so strenuously maintained. The name, he says, was very common among the Jews, and he quotes Lightfoot’s account that this man was the teacher of Paul, the son of the Simon who took the Saviour in his arms, and the grandson of the famous Hillel, known among the Jews by the title of Rabban Gamaliel the elder; he is said to have died eighteen years before the destruction of Jerusalem, and he died as he had lived, a Pharisee. There is not the least evidence, Barnes insists, that he was a friend of the Christian religion, but he was evidently a man of far more liberal views than the other members of the sanhedrim. A doctor of the law he explains as a teacher of the Jewish law, one whose province it was to interpret the laws of Moses and probably to preserve and transmit the traditional laws, so celebrated that Saul of Tarsus went to Jerusalem to receive the benefit of his instructions; and being honoured by all the people, his advice was likely to be respected. The putting forth of the apostles was done doubtless because if they had been suffered to remain it was apprehended that they would take fresh courage and be confirmed in their purposes, and besides it was customary, when the council deliberated, to command the accused to retire. Ellicott says the strict meaning of the verb describes the action of a saw, and that used figuratively it seems to imply a more lacerating pain than the pricked to the heart of the earlier chapter, leading not to repentance but to hatred; the persons spoken of are principally the high priest and his Sadducean followers. In Gamaliel he says we are brought into contact with one of the heroes of Rabbinic history, whose part in the opening of the great drama, and not less his position as the instructor of Paul, demand attention: we have to think of him as the grandson of the great Hillel, the representative of the best school of Pharisaism, the tolerant and large-hearted rival of the narrow and fanatic Shammai, whose precepts, such as that we should do nothing to another which we would not that he should do to us, remind us of the Sermon on the Mount. The fame of Hillel, he adds, won for him the highest honour of Judaism, the title of Rabban and the office of President of the Council, so that for the first time there seemed likely to be a dynasty of scribes, the office of chief of the Jewish schools, what we might almost call their Professorship of Theology, being transmitted through four generations, Hillel being succeeded by his son Simeon. Robertson parses the verb as an imperfect passive of an old verb meaning to saw in two, and says that here it is rage that cuts into their hearts and not conviction of sin as in the earlier chapter, the word occurring only here and after Stephen’s speech in the New Testament. The next verb he parses as an imperfect middle, so that they were plotting and planning to kill the apostles then and there; the point at the earlier hearing was whether the apostles deserved stoning for curing the cripple by demoniacal power, but here it was disobedience to the command of the Sanhedrin, which was not a capital offence, so that, as has been said, they were on the point of committing a grave judicial blunder.

Chrysostom observes that this Gamaliel was Paul’s teacher, and says one may well wonder how, being so right-minded in his judgment and withal learned in the law, he did not yet believe; but it cannot be, he adds, that he should have continued in unbelief to the end, and indeed it appears plainly from the words he here speaks. Observe, he says, how judiciously he frames his speech, and how he immediately at the very outset puts them in fear; and that he may not be suspected of taking their part, he addresses them as if he and they were of the same opinion, and does not use much vehemence, but as speaking to men intoxicated through passion he expresses himself as he does, warning them not to go to work rashly and in a hurry. Before he gives his examples, Chrysostom notes, he says take heed to yourselves; but when he has cited them, then he declares his opinion.

debates: How far Gamaliel leaned toward the new faith: Chrysostom cannot believe that a man so right-minded and so learned persisted in unbelief to the end, and reads the intervention itself as evidence; Lightfoot answers that he died a Pharisee and approved, if he did not write, the prayer composed against the heretics; Barnes says there is not the least evidence that he was a friend of the Christian religion, only a man of far more liberal views than the rest of the council; Clarke agrees that he probably favoured it not at all, while calling his advice humane, sensible, candid and enlightened.

What the cutting to the heart amounts to: Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all take the image from a saw, and Ellicott and Robertson both stress the contrast with the earlier scene, where the same kind of wound led to repentance rather than hatred; Calvin alone finds a positive force even here, that the word pierces the reprobate and urges their consciences, their fury springing from the sense of being arraigned by their judge.

Whether a sentence had been resolved on: Robertson says they were plotting to kill on the spot and cites the verdict that they were on the point of a grave judicial blunder, since disobedience to the Sanhedrin was no capital offence; Barnes thinks their minds were made up but doubts that any formal decree was passed.
outliers: Ellicott sets Gamaliel in the line of Hillel, the tolerant rival of the narrow and fanatical Shammai, and notes that the office passed through four generations so that there seemed likely to be a dynasty of scribes.
Lightfoot adds that Gamaliel’s son Simeon succeeded him in the chair and perished in the ruins of Jerusalem.

Chrysostom analyses the rhetoric of the speech, that Gamaliel puts the council in fear at the outset, speaks as though he shared their opinion so as not to be suspected of taking the prisoners’ part, and reserves his own advice until after the examples.
Barnes draws the general observation that the effect of the doctrines of the gospel is often to make men enraged.

36.pericope_label: For before these days rose up Theudas, boasting himself to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered, and brought to nought. After this man rose up Judas of Galilee in the days of the taxing, and drew away much people after him: he also perished; and all, even as many as obeyed him, were dispersed. And now I say unto you, Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought: but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God

schools.summary: Gill reports the Theudas of Josephus, who set up for a prophet and drew a large number after him, promising that if they would follow him to the Jordan with their goods he would divide the waters and give them passage dryshod, until Cuspius Fadus, then administering Judea, sent out troops of horse, killed many, took others and brought them in triumph to Jerusalem with the head of Theudas. This account, he says, agrees with Gamaliel’s instance and differs only in chronology, since Gamaliel’s case must have been some time before or he could not have mentioned it, whereas the story Josephus relates was several years after; some think Josephus mistaken in his chronology, and then all is right, while others suppose another Theudas is intended, one whom Origen places before the birth of Christ. Of the advice he says it is the sum of Gamaliel’s counsel upon the observation of these and other instances, and of the second branch of the dilemma that a thing is of God if it is according to the counsel of his will, a scheme of his forming and a work to which he has called men, and if they proceed in it on good principles and with a view to the honour and glory of God. Calvin observes that if we credit Josephus, Gamaliel here alters the true course of the history, since Josephus reports that Judas of Gamala raised a tumult with his adherents when Quirinius was proconsul, to prevent a census from being taken, and that Theudas boasted himself a prophet of God when Cuspius Fadus was procurator, Fadus having been sent into Judea by Claudius Caesar, the former history being recorded in the eighteenth book of the Antiquities and the other in the twentieth. But Calvin thinks that Luke did not mean to note the course of time, and that since Gamaliel brought in two like examples he might put the one in place of the other without having respect of time. Furthermore, he says, even these examples with which Gamaliel confirms his opinion do not sufficiently agree with the present cause: because Judas was not resisted at once, the sedition he had raised was the occasion of many murders, and at length he was vanquished with hand and weapon; and Theudas also would have done far more hurt had he not been put to flight in time by Cuspius Fadus. Gamaliel has respect only to this, that men have unlucky success when they advance themselves unadvisedly, and that this comes to pass by the just judgment of God; but because the priests refuse to hearken when God gives them good counsel, they are worthy to be made amazed by man with frivolous reasons, wavering hither and thither through foolish perplexity. He adds that if we cast the time, we shall find it was at least twelve years after the death of Christ before the apostles were beaten.

Lightfoot notes that Josephus makes mention of one Theudas, an impostor whose character indeed agrees well enough with this of ours, but that they seem to disagree in time, since Josephus brings in his Theudas when Fadus was governor of Judea, about the fifth or sixth year of Claudius, while Gamaliel brings in his before the times of Judas the Galilean. Those who are advocates for Josephus, he says, imagine that there might be another Theudas besides the one he mentions, but they do but imagine it, for they name none. He can instance in two more of that name, he adds, neither of which agrees with this of Gamaliel or affords any light to the chronology of Josephus, one of them a physician mentioned in the Babylonian Sanhedrin in a dispute about where Daniel was when Nebuchadnezzar’s image was set up and worshipped, that he should all that while come under no examination nor have the least harm fall to him.

Clarke observes that Josephus mentions one named Theudas who was the author of an insurrection, about whom there has been much controversy whether he were the person spoken of here by Gamaliel; every circumstance as related by Josephus agrees well enough with what is referred to here except the chronology, for the Theudas mentioned by Josephus made his insurrection when Fadus was governor of Judea, which was at least ten years after the time in which the apostles were brought before this council. Much labour, he says, has been thrown away in unsuccessful attempts to reconcile the historian and the evangelist, when it is very probable they speak of different transactions. He reports Bishop Pearce’s view that the whole difficulty will disappear if we follow the opinion of Archbishop Usher, who imagined that Luke’s Theudas was the same as that Judas of whom Josephus gives the account that a little after the death of Herod the Great he raised an insurrection in Galilee and aimed at getting the sovereignty of Judea, and that he was defeated and put to death; and that Theudas and Judas might be names for the same person Pearce thinks probable from the consideration that the same apostle who is called Judas and Jude elsewhere is called Thaddeus and Lebbeus in the Gospels, since no Jew had more than two names unless a patronymic were added, so that it is not unreasonable to suppose Thaddeus and Theudas the same name. Dr Lightfoot, he adds, thinks that Josephus has made a slip in his chronology, and rather concludes that the Theudas of the twentieth book is the person referred to in the text; but Clarke confesses the matter does not appear to him of so much consequence, since it is mentioned by Gamaliel in a careless way and Luke scrupulously gives the words of every speaker, the story being no doubt well known and no doubts formed on it by the Jewish council. We see plainly the end for which it was produced, he concludes, and we see that it answered this end most amply, and certainly we have no further concern with Gamaliel or his story. The boast he renders as saying that he was a great personage, on Pearce’s supposition setting himself up to be king of the Jews, and he notes that several respectable manuscripts and versions add the word great. The advice he paraphrases as, do not molest them, leave them to God, for if this counsel and work be of man it will come to nought like the rebellion of Theudas and that of Judas of Galilee, since whatever pretends to be done in the name of God but is not of him will have his curse and not his blessing, he whose name is prostituted by it vindicating his injured honour and avenging himself. Wesley marks the exact scope of the counsel: in a cause which is manifestly good we should immediately join, and in a cause which is manifestly evil we should immediately oppose, but in a sudden, new, doubtful occurrence this advice is eminently useful. He notes too that Gamaliel seems to correct himself, as if it were some sudden work rather than a counsel or design; and so it was, he adds, for the apostles had no counsel, plan or design of their own, but were mere instruments in the hand of God, working just as he led them from day to day.

Barnes sets out the two arguments by which Gamaliel enforced his advice, that there were cases or precedents in point and that if the thing should turn out to be of God it would be a solemn affair to be involved in the consequences of opposing him. How long before those days the transaction occurred cannot now be determined, he says, as it is not certain to what case Gamaliel refers; the name Theudas was quite common among the Jews, and of this man nothing more is known than is here recorded. He gives the account from Josephus of a Theudas in the time of Fadus, in the reign of Claudius, who persuaded a great part of the people to take their effects with him and follow him to the Jordan, telling them he was a prophet and would divide the river and lead them over, until Fadus came suddenly upon them, slew many, and took Theudas alive to be beheaded at Jerusalem; but this occurred at least ten or fifteen years after this discourse of Gamaliel. Many efforts have been made to reconcile Luke and Josephus on the supposition that they refer to the same man, and Lightfoot supposed that Josephus had made an error in chronology; but there is no reason, Barnes argues, to suppose that there is reference to the same event, and the fact that Josephus has not recorded the insurrection referred to by Gamaliel does not militate against the account in the Acts. For Luke is quite as credible an historian as Josephus; the name was common, and there is no improbability that there were two leaders of an insurrection so named, while if it is improbable the improbability would affect Josephus’s credit as much as Luke’s; it is altogether improbable that Gamaliel should refer to a case that was not well authenticated, or that Luke should record a speech of this kind unless it was delivered, when it would be so easy to detect the error; and Josephus has recorded many instances of insurrection and revolt, representing the country as in an unsettled state and by no means professing to give an account of all that occurred, saying elsewhere that there were at that time ten thousand other disorders in Judea and that Judea was full of robberies. When this Theudas lived cannot be ascertained, but as Gamaliel mentions him before Judas of Galilee it is probable that he lived not far from the time our Saviour was born, when many false prophets appeared claiming to be the Messiah; and the boast he takes as a claim to be an eminent prophet or the Messiah. The advice he explains as, cease to oppose them or to threaten them, and observes that Gamaliel inferred the outcome from the two instances he specified, which had been suppressed without any interference of the sanhedrim.
