It will be remembered, he cautions, that this is the mere advice of Gamaliel, who was not inspired, and that the opinion should not be adduced to guide us except as an instance of great shrewdness and prudence, since it is doubtless right to oppose error in the proper way and with the proper temper, not with arms or vituperation or the civil power but with argument and kind entreaty. Yet the sentiment is full of wisdom in regard to error, for the very way to exalt error into notice and confirm men in it is to oppose it in a harsh and unkind manner, and error left alone will often die away of itself, the interest of men in it ceasing as soon as it ceases to be opposed, whereas it is not so with truth. In this respect he applies the remark to the Christian religion, which has stood too long and in too many circumstances of prosperity and adversity to be of men, having been subjected to all trials from its pretended friends and real foes and still living as vigorous as ever; other kingdoms have changed and empires risen and fallen, systems of opinion have had their day and expired, but the preservation of the Christian religion unchanged through so many revolutions and fiery trials shows that it is not of men but of God, an argument which can be applied to no other system, since Christianity has been opposed in every form, confers no temporal conquests and appeals to no base and strong native passions, whereas other systems are supported by the sword and the state or by the terrors of superstition and the corrupt passions of men. From the second branch he infers that Gamaliel supposed it at least possible that this religion was divine, evincing a far more candid mind than the rest of the Jews, though it does not appear that he was entirely convinced; and the arguments which could not but stagger the sanhedrim were those drawn from the resurrection of Jesus, the miracle at Pentecost, the healing of the lame man and the release of the apostles from prison. They could not overthrow it, he says, because God has almighty power and can execute his purposes, and because he is unchanging and will not be diverted from his plans, so that the prediction of Gamaliel has been fulfilled, men having opposed Christianity in every way in vain and the more it has been crushed the more it has risen. The closing word he explains as meaning that if they continue to oppose it they may be found to have been opposing God, the word for fighting against God occurring nowhere else in the New Testament; to fight against God is to maintain an attitude of hostility against him, an attitude most fearful in its character and certain to be attended with an overthrow, and men may be said to do so when they oppose the gospel, its preaching, its plans and its influence, endeavouring to prevent its spread or to withdraw their families from it, and when they oppose the doctrines of the Bible and grow angry that the real truths of religion are preached. Ellicott places the insurrection of Josephus’s Theudas not before the taxing but in the reign of Claudius, under the procuratorship of Cuspius Fadus, ten or twelve years after this speech, and notes that the Theudas of whom he speaks claimed to be a prophet and promised to lead his followers across the Jordan, being taken and beheaded by a troop of horse. It has accordingly been inferred by some critics, he says, that we have here a blunder so portentous as to prove that the speech was made up long years after its alleged date by a writer ignorant of history, that the whole narrative of this part of the Acts is untrustworthy, and that the book requires to be sifted throughout with suspicious caution. On the other side, he urges four things: that the circumstances of the two cases are not the same, Josephus speaking of a very great multitude while Gamaliel fixes the number at about four hundred; that the name, whether taken as a form of the Aramaic Thaddaeus or the Greek Theodorus, was common enough to make more than one rebel of that name probable; that Josephus mentions no fewer than three insurrections of this type occurring shortly after the death of Herod the Great, one headed by Judas, a name interchangeable with Thaddaeus or Theudas, one by Simon, previously a slave of Herod’s, who proclaimed himself king and burnt Herod’s palaces, and one by Athronges and his four brothers, and adds that besides these there were numerous pretenders to the name of king, one of whom may well have been the Theudas of Gamaliel; and that it is hardly conceivable that a writer of Luke’s culture and general accuracy, writing in the reign of Nero, could have been guilty of such inaccuracy, still less that such a mistake should have been made by any author writing after Josephus’s history was in men’s hands, since a writer in the reign of Henry the Eighth would hardly have inverted the order of Wat Tyler and Jack Cade. The description given by Gamaliel, that he said he was some one, that is some great personage, agrees, he adds, with the vague account Josephus gives of the leaders of the revolts on Herod’s death, especially with that of Simon, who may have taken the name of Theudas as an alias to conceal his servile origin, and of whom Josephus says that he thought himself more worthy than any other of kingly power. The advice, Ellicott judges, implies something like a suppressed conviction not bold enough to utter itself, and Gamaliel takes his place in the class, at all times numerous, of waiters upon Providence, who are neutral till a cause is successful and then come forward with a tardy sympathy, but who above all shrink from committing themselves while there seems any possibility of failure; as a prudential dilemma the argument was forcible enough, since resistance was either needless or hopeless, and if needless a waste of energy, if hopeless a fatal risk. We may legitimately think of the fiery disciple, he adds, as listening impatiently to this temporising counsel and being stirred by it to greater vehemence; and he prefers the rendering it will be overthrown, so as to preserve the emphasis of the repetition of the same verb in the next clause of the dilemma. Robertson notes that Luke represents Gamaliel as speaking of a man who led a revolt before that of Judas the Galilean at the enrolment under Quirinius, whereas Josephus tells of a Theudas who led a similar insurrection in the reign of Claudius; it is not certain that Josephus and Gamaliel refer to the same Theudas, since the name is an abbreviation of Theodosus and common, and Josephus gives an account of four men named Simon who followed each other within forty years and of three named Judas within ten who were all instigators of rebellion. If the same Theudas is meant, then either Josephus or Luke has the wrong historical order, and in that case one will credit the one or the other according to his estimate of the two as reliable historians. The boast he parses as an indirect assertion with the accusative of general reference, the pronoun meaning clearly somebody of importance here; the joining he parses from a verb meaning to lean towards, occurring only here in the New Testament, and the dispersal from an old verb meaning to dissolve or go to pieces, likewise only here. The advice he renders as, do ye stand off from these men, and sums the policy as hands off; the reason gives two alternatives stated as conditional clauses, the first undetermined but with prospect of determination, so that assuming the thing is from men it will be overthrown, loosened down like a falling house, as was true of the following of Theudas and of Judas the Galilean.

debates: How the Theudas of Gamaliel relates to the Theudas of Josephus: Lightfoot supposes Josephus mistaken in his chronology and dismisses the postulated second Theudas as a bare guess; Barnes denies the two passages refer to the same man at all, arguing that the name was common, that Luke is as credible as Josephus, and that Josephus never professed to record every disorder; Clarke reports Pearce’s conjecture that Luke’s Theudas is the Judas who rose after Herod’s death, then sets the whole question aside as of little consequence; Ellicott answers the charge of a portentous blunder point by point; Robertson leaves it to the reader’s estimate of the two historians; Calvin denies that Gamaliel is narrating in order at all.

Whether Gamaliel’s examples fit his case: Calvin alone objects that they do not, since Judas was left unresisted and his sedition cost many lives, and Theudas would have done far more harm had Fadus not scattered him in time, so that the argument holds only on the general point that men who advance themselves rashly come to nothing; Barnes takes the precedents as sound and as the ground of the inference.

What the advice is worth: Barnes calls it shrewd and prudent while warning that Gamaliel was not inspired and that his opinion should not be made a rule, since error is to be opposed by argument and kind entreaty; Ellicott finds in it a suppressed conviction not bold enough to utter itself, and places Gamaliel among the perennial waiters upon Providence; Wesley limits its use to sudden and doubtful cases, since a manifestly good cause should be joined at once and a manifestly evil one opposed at once.
outliers: Ellicott answers the charge of anachronism by observing that a writer in the reign of Henry the Eighth would hardly have inverted the order of Wat Tyler and Jack Cade.

Barnes turns the second horn of the dilemma into an argument for the divine origin of Christianity, which has outlasted systems sustained by the sword, by the state and by the corrupt passions of men, and has risen the higher for being crushed.

Wesley notices that Gamaliel corrects himself in mid-sentence, calling it a work rather than a counsel, and observes that this was truer than he knew, since the apostles had no plan of their own but were instruments led from day to day.
Lightfoot adds two other bearers of the name from rabbinic sources, including a physician cited in a dispute about where Daniel was when Nebuchadnezzar’s image was worshipped.
themes: if it be of men it will come to nought

40.pericope_label: And to him they agreed: and when they had called the apostles, and beaten them, they commanded that they should not speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. And they departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name. And daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ

schools.summary: Gill says the council were convinced and persuaded by Gamaliel’s reasonings, approved his advice and agreed to follow it, and that the apostles departed having been threatened and beaten. Of the last verse he says they preached every day with great constancy and assiduity, both publicly and privately, in the temple, the place of public worship where the Jews resorted, and in each of their private houses as often as they had opportunity. Calvin observes that Gamaliel’s counsel was allowed, and yet the apostles are beaten and forbidden to teach; hereby we gather how great the rage of the enemies was, who being now pacified, or at least mitigated, yet conduct themselves so intemperately. It appears also, he says, what evil success those doubtful counsels have wherein men alone are respected and the truth of God set aside: Gamaliel obtains thus much, that the lives of the apostles may be spared, but in the meantime the Son of God is blasphemed and slandered in their person and the truth of the gospel is buried in eternal silence, so much as in the enemies lies. God surely does by this means wonderfully spread abroad his word, he grants, yet that counsel ceases not to be evil; and this we must note, because most men at this day think that they do not a little obey God if they save the lives of those who come in hazard for the doctrine of the gospel, or somewhat incline the enemies to lenity, while in the meantime they are not afraid to drive them to the wicked denial of Christ, the confessing of whom is far more precious in the sight of God than the life of all men. But what could they do, he asks, who, casting away all care of godliness, would purchase God’s favour to themselves by an act of mere humanity? Of the closing verse he says that constancy accompanied their joy, for how is it that we are discouraged with persecution save only because none lifts himself up to Christ, that he may in mind lay hold upon the fruit of victory and so be pricked forward to patience; but the man who thinks with himself that he is happy when he suffers for Christ’s sake shall never faint though he must suffer hard conflicts. Therefore the apostles are, after a sort, armed with stripes, so that they valiantly make haste to death; and woe be to our daintiness, he concludes, who, having suffered a little persecution, by and by resign the torch to another, as if we were now old worn soldiers.

Clarke says the council agreed with Gamaliel so far as not to slay the apostles nor attempt any further to imprison them, but that their malevolence could not be thus easily satisfied, and therefore they beat them, probably giving each of them thirty-nine stripes, and having commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, let them go. It was of Jesus they were afraid, he adds, not of the apostles; they plainly saw that if the doctrine of Christ was preached it must prevail, and if it prevailed they must come to nought. It was a wise saying of the popish bishops in the time of Queen Mary, he recalls, that if they did not put down printing it would put them down; they laboured to put down the printing, but they could not, and under God the printing, by exposing the wickedness of their doctrine and practices, and especially by multiplying copies of the New Testament, did most effectually put them down. The next verse he would read as, they departed rejoicing from the presence of the sanhedrin, because they there were deemed worthy to be dishonoured on account of The Name, noting that the word his is omitted by several manuscripts and versions, and that The Name probably by this time distinguished both the author of salvation and the sacred system of doctrine which the apostles preached. To rejoice in persecution and triumph in the midst of pain, shame, disgrace and various threatened deaths, he says, is the privilege of the New Testament; nothing of this kind, as far as he can recollect, appears even in the choicest saints under the Old Testament dispensation, some of whom fretted and mourned and sometimes even murmured, while some merely possessed their souls in patience, whereas Christians exulted and triumphed in the God of their salvation, which he calls no mean proof of the additional light and evidence the New Testament dispensation affords. The daily attendance in the temple he refers to the hours of morning and evening prayer, since the apostles felt it their duty to worship God in public and to help others to make a profitable use of the practice; every man who professes Christianity, he adds, should in this respect copy their conduct, nor can any man be considered to have any religion, let his sentiments be what they may, who does not attend on the public worship of his Maker. Far from desisting, he says, they became more zealous, yea incessant, in their work, taking advantage of the public assemblies in the temple as well as of all private opportunities to teach all the truths of their holy religion and to proclaim Jesus as the only Messiah, that he who was crucified rose from the dead and was exalted a Prince and a Saviour at the right hand of God. How little must these men have regarded their lives, he exclaims, who in the midst of such danger could pursue a line of conduct which to all human views must terminate in their ruin: they loved their Master, they loved his work, they loved their thankless countrymen, they loved their present wages of persecution and stripes, and hated nothing but their own lives; these men were proper persons to be employed in converting the world, and preachers of the Gospel may learn from them at once their duty, their employment and their interest. Wesley notes only that rejoicing to suffer shame is a sure mark of the truth, joy in affliction being true, deep and pure.

Barnes explains that the council were persuaded by Gamaliel only so far as their design of putting the apostles to death was concerned, abandoning that but not complying with his advice to let them entirely alone. The usual amount of lashes inflicted on offenders was thirty-nine, and beating or whipping was a common mode of punishing minor offences among the Jews, expressly foretold by the Saviour as awaiting the apostles. The reason they did not adopt the advice altogether, he says, was doubtless that they feared their authority would be despised by the people: they had commanded the apostles not to preach, they had threatened them and imprisoned them, and now, if they suffered them to go without even the appearance of punishment, it would be supposed that the apostles had triumphed over the sanhedrim; it is probable also that they were so indignant that they could not suffer them to go without the gratification of subjecting them to the public odium of a whipping, since men, if they cannot accomplish their full purposes of malignity against the gospel, will take up with even some petty annoyance rather than let it alone. Of the rejoicing he observes that nothing to most men would seem more disgraceful than a public whipping, a punishment inflicted not so much because it gives pain as because it is esteemed to be attended with disgrace, and that the Jewish rulers doubtless desired the apostles to be so affected by the shame as to be unwilling to appear again in public or to preach the gospel any more, yet in this they were disappointed and the effect was just the reverse. He gives six reasons why the apostles rejoiced: that they were permitted to imitate the example of the Lord Jesus, who had been scourged and reviled; that by this they had evidence that they were his friends and followers, engaged in the same cause and enduring the same sufferings; that they had been told to expect this as a part of their enterprise; that religion appears to a Christian so excellent and lovely that he is willing for its sake to endure trial and persecution and death; that Christians show attachment to Christ by being willing to suffer for him and to share his persecutions; and that the apostles were engaged in a cause of innocence, truth and benevolence, and so rejoiced in a conscience void of offence, since when others disgrace themselves by vile conduct towards us we should not feel that the disgrace belongs to us. Counted worthy he takes to mean esteemed fit for it by the sanhedrim, and he is careful to say that it does not mean that God esteemed them worthy but that the Jewish council judged them fit to suffer shame in this cause. To suffer shame he explains as to be dishonoured in the estimation of the Jewish rulers, the particular disgrace here being the whipping, and he remarks that a profession of the Christian religion has been in all ages esteemed by many to be a disgrace, because Jesus is himself despised, because his precepts are opposed to the gaiety and follies of the world, because it attacks that on which men of the world pride themselves, because it requires a spirit which the world esteems mean and grovelling, and because it requires duties which the men of the world despise; the kinds of disgrace to which Christians have been subjected he calls too numerous to mention, from loss of property and reputation and the terrors of the dungeon and the stake to the ridicule of friends and the sneer that still tears their feelings, one main design of persecution having been to select a kind of punishment so disgraceful as to deter others from professing religion. Ellicott says the Sadducees, after their manner, would probably have preferred a more violent course, but the Pharisees were strong in the Sanhedrin and the middle way recommended by Gamaliel was under such circumstances likely to command a majority, and was therefore apparently accepted without a division; in the beating he traces the action of Caiaphas and the priests, who were not content without some punishment being inflicted, the party of Gamaliel apparently acquiescing in this as a compromise in the hope of averting more violent measures. This, he adds, is to be noted as the first actual experience of persecution falling on the whole company of the Twelve and not on Peter and John only; they were probably convicted of the minor offence of causing a disturbance in the Temple, though dismissed as with a verdict of not proven on the graver charge of heresy, and the punishment in such a case would probably be the forty stripes save one of Deuteronomy. The emotion of the next verse he says is probably in one sense natural to all who have an intense conviction of the Truth for which they suffer, but in this case there was something more, since the Twelve could not fail to remember their Lord’s beatitudes and now for the first time felt that they could rejoice and be exceeding glad because they were suffering as the prophets had suffered before them; and they were suffering for his Name, or rather, with the best manuscripts, for the Name, that of the Master who had loved them and whom they had learnt to love. The daily teaching he places, as before, probably in the Portico of Solomon, the captain of the Temple now acting on the resolution just taken and letting the movement take its course without interruption; and he prefers at home to in every house, and renders the second verb as to declare the good tidings, the word being literally to evangelise. Robertson parses the agreement as a first aorist passive of the verb to persuade, so that they were persuaded by him, and observes that Gamaliel’s shrewd advice scored against the Sadducaic contention; the Sanhedrin repeated the prohibition which the apostles had steadily refused to obey, standing by their guns but refusing to shoot, so that it was a draw with Gamaliel as tactical victor over the Sadducees, and the disciples were clearly set free because only the Sadducees had become enraged while the Pharisees held aloof. Of the last verse he notes the accusative of extent of time, all through every day, and calls it a distinct triumph to go back to the temple where they had been arrested, and at home or from house to house as it probably means; it was a great day for the disciples in Jerusalem, and they kept it up, the imperfect showing that they did not cease. Jesus, he adds, is the direct object of the participles for teaching and evangelising while the Christ is the predicate accusative, so that these words give the substance of the early apostolic preaching, that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah of promise; Gamaliel had opened the prison doors for them and they took full advantage of the opportunity that was now theirs.

debates: Whether Gamaliel’s counsel was good: Calvin alone refuses to admire it, holding that doubtful counsels in which men alone are considered and God’s truth set aside come to no good, since the lives are spared while the gospel is buried in silence so far as the enemies can manage; Robertson calls the outcome a draw with Gamaliel the tactical victor over the Sadducees; Ellicott treats it as the middle course a Pharisaic majority could carry without a division.

What counted worthy means: Barnes is careful to restrict it, that the words say the council judged them fit to suffer shame and not that God esteemed them worthy; Ellicott hears the beatitude behind the phrase and takes the suffering as an honour, as does Clarke, who would render it that they were deemed worthy to be dishonoured on account of the Name.

Whose act the scourging was: Ellicott assigns it specifically to Caiaphas and the priests, with Gamaliel’s party acquiescing as the price of a compromise; Barnes assigns it to the whole council’s fear that their authority would be despised if the apostles went free unpunished; Clarke locates the fear elsewhere, that it was Jesus and not the apostles whom the council feared.
outliers: Clarke matches the council’s calculation with the Marian bishops who said that if they did not put down printing it would put them down, and who laboured to do so and could not.
Barnes remarks that men who cannot accomplish their full malignity against the gospel will take up even some petty annoyance rather than let it alone.

Clarke claims the temper of rejoicing under persecution as a New Testament privilege, since the choicest saints of the older dispensation fretted or mourned or at best possessed their souls in patience, whereas Christians exulted.

Calvin turns the constancy into a rebuke of his own generation, that the apostles were armed by their stripes while we, having borne a little persecution, resign the torch to another as though we were worn-out soldiers.
